title: Church and Empire: An 8-Week Study
subtitle: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study on how the church relates to political power, from a denarius in a trap to the end of Christendom, keeping the crucified King above every throne.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who feel the ground shifting under the faith in their country and want to know what is actually dying and what is not. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on the long marriage of church and empire, from the coin held up to trap Jesus, through the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West. It defines the hard words plainly, never sneers at the believer who grieves the change, and is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the people who want to seize the culture or the people who want to flee it. It catches both. It asks the Christian reaching for the levers of the state whether he has confused a borrowed majority with the work of the Spirit, and it asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat by the name of holiness. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has preached the render line as a permission slip, he has flags on his own platform he has not moved, he grieves the Sunday-closed store he grew up with, and he writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means
sessions.aim: To recover the render line as a fence around a coin rather than a wall between faith and public life, and to ask what we have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his.
sessions.summary: They brought Jesus a coin because they wanted him dead. The Pharisees and the Herodians, who agreed on almost nothing, agreed to set a trap with a single question about a denarius. Pay tax to Caesar, or not. Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. We have turned the most dangerous sentence in the Gospels into a permission slip, two tidy drawers, one for politics and one for prayer, and Bell admits he has preached it that way and was wrong. Look at what Jesus does. He asks whose image is on the coin, and the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word Genesis uses when the man is made in the image of God. The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back. But the thing that bears the image of God is the person holding the coin. Render to God the things that are God's, and the thing that is God's is you. Bell grants the strong version of the comfortable reading first, that the two-drawer instinct kept the church from becoming the state after centuries of religious war, and Caesar really does have a domain. The question is its size. The line does not divide reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian saw it. Render the coin to Caesar and yourself to God, for if all things are Caesar's, what will be left for God. They killed him anyway, charged with forbidding tribute and making himself a king. The verse we use to make God small was spoken to make Caesar small.

keyScripture.why: The render line was spoken to spring a trap, and instead of dividing faith from public life it puts a fence around a coin and gives every image-bearer to God.

discussion.q: Before tonight, how had you heard the render line used, and what did it seem to permit?
discussion.behind: Surface the comfortable reading before dismantling it. Most will have heard it as keep your faith out of politics or keep your head down. The point is not to shame the reading but to show the whole room arrived holding the same tidy drawers, so the reversal has somewhere to land. Land it on recognition, not on cleverness.

discussion.q: Bell points out the coin bears Caesar's image but the person holding it bears God's. What changes when you weigh the two drawers instead of assuming they are equal?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the whole session. If everything bearing God's image belongs to God, Caesar's drawer holds metal and God's drawer holds every person who ever lived. Help them feel that the line does not split reality in half. It fences a coin and hands the rest to God.

discussion.q: The two-drawer reading protected real things, keeping the church from becoming the state after Europe bled over religion. How do we honor what it got right while seeing what it hid?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness early. The separation instinct is wisdom paid for in blood, not cowardice. You want the room to grant Caesar a real domain before they shrink it, so the conclusion does not sound like the church grabbing for power instead of Rome.

discussion.q: Bell says a church with no power reads the line as a sword and a church with power reads it as a truce, and we have read it as a truce for sixteen centuries. Why would safety change how we hear the same words?
discussion.behind: You want them to see that the words did not change, the reader did. The same sentence that sounded like a sword in the year 64 sounds like a settlement in a comfortable hand. The cost of meaning it is what we lost. Tie this to how easily we domesticate dangerous texts.

discussion.q: Bell ends by asking what we have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his, our final allegiance, our sense of who holds history. What comes to mind when you sit with that question honestly?
discussion.behind: Move from interpretation to self-implication, including the leader. You are not hunting confessions to shame anyone. You want each person to name one place their deepest trust has slid toward a power they can see. Go first if the room is slow.

objections.objection: This is just a way to drag the church into politics. Jesus told us to render to Caesar so we would stay in our lane and keep faith private.
objections.response: Sit with what the lane reading protects before answering. It guarded against the church becoming the state, and that is a real mercy. Then make the distinction gently. Bell is not arguing the church should seize Caesar's throne. He is arguing the line keeps Caesar out of the human soul, not faith out of public life. You can honor that the coin goes back and still refuse to let the emperor have the one thing he most wants, the last word over a creature made in the image of God.

objections.objection: Fine, then everything belongs to God, so a faithful Christian should resist paying taxes and treat the government as Pharaoh.
objections.response: Bell rules this out as plainly as the other error. Jesus did not lead a tax revolt, the coin goes back, and Scripture tells us to honor the emperor in the same breath it tells us to fear God. The render line relativizes Caesar without abolishing him. The point is not to treat every government as an enemy but to refuse the one allegiance that belongs to God alone. Pay the tax. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one ordinary loyalty in your life that you have never stopped to ask whether it belongs to Caesar or to God?
sessions.practice: This week, when you pull out a card or a bill to pay for something, let it become a small examination. Ask what else you have been handing over without noticing, your final hope, your sense of who is in charge. Do not fix it. Just notice where your allegiance went and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have used a hard sentence to make ourselves comfortable, and we have handed you the small change while keeping the throne of ourselves. Forgive us for the parts of our hope we have minted in Rome. You stamped your image on us, and we belong to you, not to Caesar, not to a party, not to our own fear dressed up as prudence. Give the coin back to the world this week, and give all of ourselves to you. In the name of the King the empire could not keep buried, amen.
reflection: Where have I read a dangerous text as a domestic one because I no longer stand anywhere it would cost me something to mean it?
What have I quietly placed in Caesar's drawer that bears the image of God and was never his to hold?
If my final allegiance were tested tomorrow, do I actually know where it would land, or have I arranged my life so the trap never springs?
sessions.teaching: Start where the trap started, because the setting is half the meaning. They brought Jesus a coin because they wanted him dead. The Pharisees and the Herodians agreed on almost nothing, yet they agreed to walk up together with one question about a denarius. Pay tax to Caesar, or not. Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. There was no safe answer, and that is what a trap is for. Hold that in mind, because we have taken the most dangerous sentence in the Gospels and turned it into a permission slip. Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, and we hear two tidy drawers, one for politics, one for prayer. I have preached it that way, as if Jesus came to teach us how to keep our heads down, and I was wrong, and the text knew it before I did. Now watch what he actually does. He asks for the coin, because he does not carry one. He asks whose image is on it, and they say Caesar's, and the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis when the man is made in the image of God. The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back. But the question hanging in the air, the one the trappers do not see coming, is what bears the image of God. The answer is the person holding the coin. Render to God the things that are God's, and the thing that is God's is you. Before you press that point, give the comfortable reading its full weight, because it is not stupid. The two-drawer reading protected real things for centuries. It kept the church from becoming the state and the state from becoming the church. After Europe bled over confession in the wars of religion, the instinct to separate the spheres looked like mercy, and it was. Caesar has a domain. Taxes are real. The coin goes back. Jesus did not lead a tax revolt, and Scripture tells us to honor the emperor in the same breath it tells us to fear God. So answer the strong version, not the weak one. Yes, Caesar has a domain. The question is its size. The two-drawer reading assumes the drawers are roughly equal, God with the soul and Caesar with the body and the budget and the army. But weigh the sentence. If everything bearing God's image belongs to God, then Caesar's drawer holds metal stamped with his face, and God's drawer holds every person who ever lived, including Caesar. The line does not divide reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian saw it plainly. Render the coin to Caesar and yourself to God, for if all things are Caesar's, what will be left for God. They killed him anyway. The charge at the cross is the very one the trap was built to produce, that he forbade tribute to Caesar and made himself a king. Rome was not fooled by a clever answer. Rome understood, better than the modern reader does, that a man who says the emperor is made in the image of a higher King has not stayed out of politics. He has refused the emperor the one thing the emperor most demands, the last word. Here is the thing to land in the room. A church with no power reads this line as a sword. A church with power reads it as a truce. We have read it as a truce for sixteen centuries, and that is exactly the period in which we forgot what it cost. The difference is not in the words. It is in who is reading them and what it costs the reader to mean them. So the trap meant for Jesus springs instead on us. Not whether you will pay your taxes. You will, and you should. The question is what you have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his. Your final allegiance. Your sense of who holds history. The part of you that votes its fear and calls it prudence. Give the coin back. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.

scriptureStudy.note: The Pharisees and the Herodians come together, two factions who hate each other, united only by wanting Jesus gone. Watch who has to ally to trap him. The trap is the whole frame of the saying.
They open with flattery, you are true and do not care about appearances. Flattery is the oil on the hinge of a trap. The compliment is the bait before the question that has no safe answer.

Jesus names it for what it is, why put me to the test. He will not pretend the question is sincere. He asks them to bring a denarius, and the fact that they can produce one inside the temple precincts already convicts them.
Whose image and inscription is this. The word for image is eikon, the same word Genesis uses for the man made in God's image. The whole answer is hidden in that one word, waiting.

God created man in his own image, in the eikon of God he created him. Set this beside the coin. The coin bears Caesar's image and goes back to Caesar. The person bears God's image and goes back to God.
Render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. The sentence does not split reality down the middle. It fences a coin and hands every image-bearer to God, which is nearly everything.
The charge at the cross, that he forbids tribute to Caesar and calls himself a king. The render line did not get Jesus off the hook. Rome heard the subversion the comfortable reader misses.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into what the denarius actually was, because the object carried a claim. The coin in circulation bore the image of Tiberius and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, a small confession of imperial divinity carried in every pocket. To a faithful Jew it was a portable idol, which is part of why the Pharisees objected to the tax on religious grounds while the Herodians profited from the arrangement. When Jesus asks them to produce one, the request itself exposes that his accusers carry the idol he does not. Then take up the contested history of the two-drawer reading. William Cavanaugh argues in The Myth of Religious Violence that the tidy separation of religious and secular was not a neutral discovery but a story the emerging state told to justify absorbing the loyalties the church once held, presenting itself as the cool referee that ended religious violence. A careful group should hold that thesis at its weight, neither swallowing it whole nor dismissing it, and ask whether our instinct to privatize faith is Christian wisdom or a settlement we accepted from a rival power. Set N.T. Wright's reading alongside it, that the confession Jesus is Lord was never a private devotional sentiment because everyone in the first century knew the unspoken second clause, Caesar is not. The seminary-trained group should work the difference between relativizing Caesar and abolishing him, since the same passage that shrinks the emperor also commands the tax. The aim is a fence around the coin, not a torch to the throne.
sessions.caseStudy: A thoughtful member of your group, a quiet professional who avoids conflict, has clearly found relief in the comfortable reading. When you press it, he pushes back gently. He says he has always loved this verse precisely because it lets him keep his faith out of the office, off his social feeds, away from the dinner table where his family fights about politics. He keeps his head down, votes privately, and figures the render line blesses exactly that, a Christianity that minds its own business and renders the public square to Caesar. He is not grasping for power. He is doing the opposite. He has handed the whole of public life to Caesar and called the surrender obedience. Here is the leader's task. Honor the real wisdom in his instinct, because a faith that becomes a culture war is its own disease and he is right to fear it. But show him gently that the line he loves was never a wall between faith and public life. It was a fence around a coin, and everything bearing God's image, including the conversations he flees, sits on the side that belongs to God. Retreat is not the same as render.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus said to them, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. And they marveled at him.

devotional.title: Why They Brought the Coin
devotional.body: Begin with the motive, because we lose it the moment we quote the line. They did not bring Jesus a coin to learn something. They brought it to kill him. The Pharisees and the Herodians agreed on almost nothing, but they agreed to set a trap, and the trap was a question with no safe answer. Say pay the tax and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say do not and hand Rome a charge of treason. We have taken a sentence forged in a death trap and softened it into a tidy rule for keeping faith private. Before you decide what the render line means, sit with the danger it was born inside. A sentence spoken to escape execution reads differently than a maxim printed on a mug. The people who first heard it were watching to see a man die. Today, resist the instinct to make the words of Jesus comfortable. Ask whether you have taken his hardest sayings and filed them in the safe drawer, the one that asks nothing of you. The render line was never safe. It was a man refusing a trap by naming a deeper truth the trappers could not survive. Let it be dangerous again before you let it be a comfort.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have made your hardest words into easy ones and called it understanding. Give me back the danger of what you actually said. Let me hear the render line where it was spoken, in the shadow of a cross.

devotional.title: Whose Image
devotional.body: Jesus asks for the coin and asks whose image is on it. Caesar's, they say, and the matter seems settled. But the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word Genesis uses when God makes the man in his own image. The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back to Caesar. But the question that hangs in the air is what bears the image of God, and the answer is the person holding the coin. Render to God the things that are God's, and the thing that is God's is you. This is not a small point of vocabulary. It is the hinge of the whole exchange. Caesar may stamp his face on metal and call it his. He cannot stamp his face on you. You were minted in a different place, marked with a different likeness, and you belong to the one whose image you carry. Today, look at the people around you, the ones who annoy you and the ones who frighten you and the ones you would rather not see, and remember that every one of them bears the eikon of God. None of them belongs to Caesar. None of them belongs to a party. Each one is stamped with a likeness no empire can claim. Live today as a person who knows whose image he carries.
devotional.prayer: Father, you stamped your image on me and on every person I will meet today. Let me hand Caesar the coin and never the creature. Help me see your likeness where I least want to look.

devotional.title: The Size of Caesar's Drawer
devotional.body: The comfortable reading is not stupid, and we should not pretend otherwise. It kept the church from becoming the state and the state from becoming the church, and after Europe bled over religion that instinct looked like mercy. Caesar really does have a domain. Taxes are real. Peter tells us to honor the emperor in the same breath he tells us to fear God, so a faith that treats every government as Pharaoh has misread its own book. The question is not whether Caesar has a drawer. He does. The question is its size. We assume the two drawers are roughly equal, God with the soul and Caesar with the body and the budget and the nation. But if everything bearing God's image belongs to God, Caesar's drawer holds coins, and God's drawer holds every person alive. Today, practice the honor Peter commands without the worship he forbids. Pay what you owe. Respect the office. Pray for those in authority. And underneath all of it, keep clear that the emperor's reach ends at the edge of the coin, that your final allegiance was never his to ask for. Honor Caesar fully in his small and real domain, and reserve for God the vast remainder, which is almost everything, including yourself.
devotional.prayer: Lord, teach me to honor the emperor without enthroning him, to pay what I owe and keep what is yours. Show me the true size of Caesar's drawer, so small, and the true size of yours.

devotional.title: A Sword or a Truce
devotional.body: The same sentence reads two ways depending on who holds it. A church with no power hears the render line as a sword, a refusal to give the emperor the last word. A church with power hears it as a truce, a property line that lets it keep both drawers. We have read it as a truce for sixteen centuries, which is exactly the period in which we forgot what it cost. Remember that they killed him anyway. The charge at the cross was the very one the trap was designed to produce, that he forbade tribute and made himself a king. Rome was not fooled by a clever answer. Rome understood that a man who tells you the emperor bears the image of a higher King has not stayed out of politics. He has refused the emperor the one thing the emperor most wants. Today, ask which way you have been reading the words of Jesus. Have you turned his dangerous sayings into settlements because you no longer stand anywhere they would cost you something. The render line sounded like a sword in the year 64 and a truce in our comfortable hands, and the difference was never in the words. It was in what it cost the reader to mean them. Ask God to let his words cost you something again.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have read your sword as a truce because I stand somewhere safe. Take me to where your words cost something. Let me mean the render line the way the martyrs meant it.

devotional.title: What You Handed Over
devotional.body: In the wilderness the tempter showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offered them for a single bow, and Jesus refused, because the kingdoms were not worth the worship. The render trap is the same offer in a smaller key. Give Caesar the coin, yes, but the trap wanted Jesus to give Caesar the allegiance too, and that he would not do. So the question the trap meant to spring on him springs instead on us. Not whether you will pay your taxes, because you will, and the kingdom does not rise or fall on a denarius. The question is what you have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his. Your final hope. Your sense of who holds history. The part of you that votes its fear instead of its faith and calls the fear prudence. We sorted ourselves into Caesar's drawer and told ourselves we were being responsible. End the week with the honest inventory. Find one ordinary loyalty you have never stopped to weigh, and ask whether it belongs to Caesar or to God. Then give the coin back to the world, and give all of yourself to the one whose image you bear. Keep nothing of yourself in the emperor's hand.
devotional.prayer: Father, I have handed you the small change and kept the throne of myself, and I have given Caesar things that were only ever yours. Forgive the parts of my hope I minted in Rome. Take back all of me, who bear your image and belong to you alone. Amen.

sessions.title: Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
sessions.aim: To separate Christendom, the social arrangement, from Christianity, the body of people who confess a crucified Lord, and to grieve the right one.
sessions.summary: A pastor Bell respects told him the country is losing its faith and meant it as a funeral. The polls back him up. Attendance falls, the category of no religion grows fastest, and the assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has thinned to almost nothing. Bell grieved too, for a while, until he noticed they were grieving two different things and using one word for both. There is Christianity, the people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who walked out of a tomb. And there is Christendom, the arrangement in which that confession is the default setting of a civilization, baked into its laws and calendar and manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same act. One is dying. The other has survived the death of empires before. Bell carries the mustard seed, the smallest of seeds that becomes a tree, and notes the parable promises growth from smallness, not ownership of the field. He grants the strong defense of Christendom, that it built hospitals and universities and a moral grammar the secular world still borrows without paying, and O'Donovan is right that the gospel genuinely reshaped political authority. But the same arrangement built a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ, and Kierkegaard called that the great illusion, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross. The arrangement has a date, 312, the night before the Milvian Bridge, and by 380 Nicene Christianity was the official religion of the state. The end of Christendom is not the defeat of the church. It is the return of the church to the only conditions under which it has ever known how to grow.

keyScripture.why: Jesus describes the kingdom as the smallest of seeds that grows into a tree, promising life from smallness rather than ownership of the field, which Christendom forgot.

discussion.q: Bell says we use one word, Christianity, for two different things, the faith and the cultural arrangement. In your own life, where do you see the two getting confused?
discussion.behind: Open by getting the distinction into the room in plain terms. The faith is people who confess a crucified Lord. Christendom is the setting where that confession is the default. Help them name a place they have treated cultural Christianity and living faith as the same thing, because the rest of the session depends on telling them apart.

discussion.q: The mustard seed parable promises growth from smallness, not ownership of the field. Why did the church spend centuries assuming Jesus meant the empire anyway?
discussion.behind: You want them to feel the gap between what Jesus described and what the church became. He pointed to the smallest thing in the garden. We built the largest thing in the empire and called it the same. Let them sit in how strange that substitution is once you see it.

discussion.q: Bell grants that Christendom built real goods, hospitals, universities, a moral grammar the secular world still borrows. How do we honor those goods while still refusing to grieve the wrong thing?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The defenders of Christendom are not cartoon theocrats, they are people who saw what replaces a Christian frame and found it wanting. Make sure no one who grieves the change feels mocked before the harder point lands, that the same arrangement made faith cheap.

discussion.q: Kierkegaard called Christendom a nation of Christians none of whom had met the offense of the cross. Where have you seen faith made cheap simply because it was the default?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. When faith is the default, the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Help them recognize, without contempt, that some of what is falling away now is the nominal and the inherited, an honesty arriving late rather than a pure tragedy.

discussion.q: Bell admits part of him wants the old scaffolding back, the full pews, the easier job, even knowing habit and respectability filled those pews. Where do you feel that same pull?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first. The honest confession is that we miss the advantage and call it missing the faith. Invite people to name what they actually grieve, and to ask whether it is Christ or comfort, without rushing anyone to a tidy answer.

objections.objection: This is a convenient way to celebrate the collapse of Christian culture. The decline of faith is a tragedy, and calling it freedom is just spiritualizing defeat.
objections.response: Bell feels the loss honestly and refuses to flatten it. He has five sons inheriting a thinner world, and he says grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those, because they are good. The point is narrower. Cultural Christianity is not the same as the church, and what is dying is partly the nominal and the convenient. You can mourn the real losses without putting the church in the coffin, because the seed is still in the ground.

objections.objection: If Christendom built the hospitals and the universities and the moral grammar, then pulling out the Christian root will rot the fruit, so we should defend the arrangement, not bury it.
objections.response: Grant the strong version fully, because O'Donovan is right that the West was bent by the gospel into new shapes of mercy and law. The question is whether the church protected those goods by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery. A consensus held by habit is always one generation from collapse. The answer is not to defend the throne but to form a people who would still live the mercy when the culture no longer requires it. That is the church the early centuries actually produced.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture the faith you want to hand to the next generation, are you picturing a culture that supports it or a community that lives it?
sessions.practice: This week, notice one thing you have always assumed was Christian about your surroundings, a phrase, a holiday, a habit, a closed store. Ask whether it points anyone to the crucified Lord or simply to a culture that used to call itself by his name. Bring what you find back next time.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the small seed, we have mistaken the tree we built for the kingdom you planted, and we have grieved the loss of our advantage as though it were the loss of you. Teach us to tell the difference between the church and the culture that wore its clothes. Where cheap faith is falling away, give us the costly kind that has met the offense of the cross. You grew your church under a hostile empire once. Grow it in us again. Amen.
reflection: What am I actually grieving when I grieve the change in my country, the loss of Christ or the loss of an advantage?
Where has the faith been cheap in me because it was the default, never tested against the offense of the cross?
If every cultural support for my faith were gone tomorrow, what of it would still be standing, and what would that tell me?
sessions.teaching: Begin with the funeral, because that is how the loss feels to honest people. A pastor I respect told me the country is losing its faith, and he meant it as a death. The polls back him up. Attendance falls. The category of no religion grows fastest. The cultural assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has thinned to almost nothing. He grieved, and so did I, for a while. Then I noticed we were grieving two different things and using one word for both. There is Christianity, the body of people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who walked out of a tomb. And there is Christendom, the social arrangement in which that confession is the default setting of a civilization, baked into the laws and the calendar and the manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same act. One is dying. The other has survived the death of empires before. Carry the parable that is older than the problem. The kingdom of God is like a grain of mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which becomes a tree where the birds nest. Notice what it does not promise. It does not promise the tree will own the field, pass the laws, or seat the king. It promises growth from smallness, life from something you could lose in the dirt. Jesus described his movement as the smallest thing in the garden, not the largest thing in the empire, and we spent sixteen centuries assuming he meant the empire anyway. Now give the strong defense its full hearing, because the defenders of Christendom are not power-drunk theocrats. They have looked at what replaces a Christian frame and found it wanting. They point out, correctly, that the hospital and the university and the very idea that the weak have worth grew in soil Christendom tilled. Oliver O'Donovan makes the serious case that political authority itself was reshaped by the gospel, that the West was bent by Christianity into new shapes of mercy and law. When such people grieve, they grieve something real. A scaffolding is coming down, and scaffolding holds things up. So answer the strong version. Yes, Christendom built hospitals and universities and a moral grammar the secular world still borrows without paying. But the same arrangement built something the gospel never asked for, a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ. When faith is the default, faith is cheap, and the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Kierkegaard called it the great illusion of Christendom, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross, because everyone was already a Christian the way everyone was already Danish. The thing dying now is partly the thing he was trying to kill from the inside. Trace the root to a date. The arrangement begins around 312, the night before the Milvian Bridge, when Constantine reportedly saw a sign and won an empire and handed the church the keys to the city it had been dying outside of. By 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the state. In three generations the faith went from a persecuted minority burying its martyrs in secret to the establishment that could persecute in turn. That was a genuine mercy after the slaughter, and it was also the moment the mustard seed got mistaken for the cedar. Here is the reversal the grieving pastor could not see. The end of Christendom is not the defeat of the church. It is the return of the church to the only conditions under which it has ever known how to grow. I feel the loss honestly. I have five sons inheriting a thinner world, and part of me wants the old scaffolding back, the full pews, the easier job. But I have to be honest about what filled those pews. Habit filled them. Respectability filled them. Those are not the gospel. So grieve the right thing. Grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those. But do not grieve the death of cultural Christianity as though the church were in the coffin. The seed is still in the ground.

scriptureStudy.note: The kingdom is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man sows. The first word about the kingdom is smallness and hiddenness, a seed put into the ground and lost from sight, not a banner raised over a capital.
It is the smallest of seeds and becomes a tree where the birds nest. The growth is real and even large, but it comes from below, from burial and patience, not from seizing the field.
The seed sprouts and grows, the man knows not how. The kingdom advances by a hidden life the farmer cannot engineer. Christendom forgot this and tried to manufacture the growth by law and calendar.
The kingdom is like leaven hidden in flour until it leavens the whole. Leaven works invisibly and from within, the opposite of an establishment that works by visible power and from above.

We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block and folly, but the power of God. A crucified Lord cannot be the mascot of a comfortable culture, because the comfortable, established culture is the one that crucified him.

A chosen people, sojourners and exiles. The earliest self-understanding is not establishment but exile, a distinct people passing through, which is the posture the post-Christendom church is relearning.

sessions.goingDeeper: Work the historiography of the Constantinian shift honestly rather than reaching for the version that flatters your instinct. The popular Christian story treats 312 as either a glorious triumph or a simple fall, and both are too clean. Peter Leithart in Defending Constantine argues against the tidy declension narrative, insisting the emperor's conversion was more genuine and its effects more mixed than the critics of Christendom allow, and a careful group should let that counter-voice stand against Hauerwas rather than dismissing it. Set it beside Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon in Resident Aliens, who read the end of the Constantinian arrangement not as a death to mourn but as the freeing of the church to be faithful again, a colony of resident aliens whose very existence is its witness. The advanced move is to ask what each account assumes about how God works in history, whether through the rise and reach of Christian institutions or through a faithful remnant that does not need them. Then bring in Lesslie Newbigin, who came home to England in 1974 after decades as a missionary in India and found his own country a pagan culture with Christian memories. His question reframes the whole session. How does the gospel address a culture that thinks it already knows what the gospel is and has moved on. A seminary group should weigh the difference between a missionary posture and a restorationist one, between asking how to re-evangelize a post-Christian West and asking how to recapture its institutions, and notice that Bell affirms public engagement while refusing the recapture. The genuine goods O'Donovan names are not the question. How the church holds them is.
sessions.caseStudy: A respected older couple in your group, faithful for decades, grieve the change in the country with real tears. The wife says she does not recognize the world her grandchildren are growing up in, that the stores stay open on Sunday and the schools teach things she cannot abide, and she has started giving to a ministry that promises to put Christian leaders back in charge of the culture, to win back the country for God. She is not retreating. She is reaching, hard, for the levers. Her grief is honest and her love for her grandchildren is real, and you must say so plainly before anything else. But the session presses a gentle question into her hands. Is she grieving the loss of Christ, or the loss of an advantage. The arrangement she wants back filled the pews with habit and respectability as much as with faith, and it built a Christianity people could inherit without ever meeting Christ. Do not shame her longing. Show her that the church grew fastest with every cultural lever pulling the other way, and that a faith propped up by the culture was always one generation from collapse. The recapture she funds is not the same as the kingdom she loves.

memoryVerse.text: The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree.

devotional.title: Two Words for One Thing
devotional.body: A pastor told me the country is losing its faith, and he meant it as a funeral. I grieved with him, until I noticed we were grieving two different things with one word. There is Christianity, the people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who left a tomb empty. And there is Christendom, the arrangement in which that confession is simply the default of a civilization, baked into its laws and calendar so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same act. Paul tells the Colossians their life is hidden with Christ in God. Hidden. Not displayed in the laws, not propped up by the calendar, not guaranteed by the culture, but hidden in God where no shift in the polls can reach it. Today, do the careful work of telling the two apart in your own heart. When you feel the ground shifting under the faith in your country, ask which thing is actually moving. Is it your life hidden with Christ, which nothing can touch, or is it the cultural arrangement that made the faith convenient. They are not the same, and confusing them will make you grieve a death that is not happening and miss the life that cannot die.
devotional.prayer: Lord, my life is hidden with you, and no poll or election can reach it there. Help me tell the church from the culture that wore its clothes. Let me grieve the right thing and trust the life that cannot die.

devotional.title: The Smallest Seed
devotional.body: Jesus described his kingdom as a grain of mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, lost in the dirt before it became a tree. Notice what the picture does not promise. It does not promise the tree will own the field or pass the laws or seat the king. It promises growth from smallness, life from a thing you could lose in your hand. He pointed to the smallest thing in the garden, and we spent centuries building the largest thing in the empire and calling it the same. The substitution is so strange you can miss it until someone names it. We took a parable about hiddenness and patience and turned it into a program of cultural dominance. The kingdom comes the way a seed comes, buried, quiet, slow, and from below. Today, examine where you have demanded that the kingdom come the way an empire comes, large and fast and from above. Where have you measured the health of the faith by its visibility, its market share, its grip on the culture, when Jesus measured it by a seed. Ask God to give you the patience of a gardener rather than the anxiety of a general. The seed does not need the field. It needs only to be in the ground, and it is.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you made your kingdom small as a seed, and I keep wanting it large as an empire. Give me the patience of the gardener and not the anxiety of the general. Let me trust the seed in the ground.

devotional.title: When Faith Is Cheap
devotional.body: Kierkegaard called Christendom the great illusion, a nation of Christians none of whom had met the offense of the cross, because everyone was already a Christian the way everyone was already Danish. When faith is the default, faith is cheap. When the whole culture calls itself Christian, the word stops meaning anyone in particular. The risen Christ says to the church at Sardis that they have a reputation for being alive but are dead. A name is not a pulse. A culture can hand you the name Christian the way it hands you a nationality, and you can carry it your whole life without the thing it names ever having touched you. This is the uncomfortable mercy hidden in the decline. Some of what is falling away now is the nominal and the inherited, the people who never believed no longer pretending. That is honesty arriving late, not pure tragedy. Today, ask the hard question of yourself before you ask it of the culture. Where has your own faith been cheap because it cost nothing, default because everyone around you shared it, a name without a pulse. Do not answer to condemn yourself. Answer so the living thing can be distinguished from the inherited reputation, and so what is real in you can be fed and what is only a name can be repented.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you know the difference between a name and a pulse, and I do not always. Show me where my faith has been cheap because it cost nothing. Make the living thing in me real, and let the rest fall away.

devotional.title: What Filled the Pews
devotional.body: I want the old scaffolding back, if I am honest. The full pews, the easier job, the closed store on Sunday that still meant something. But I have to be honest about what filled those pews. Habit filled them. Respectability filled them. The fear of being the odd family on the street filled them. Those are not the gospel. They are the things the gospel has to compete with, and Christendom hid the competition by dressing them in the same clothes. Hosea hears God ask what to do with a people whose love is like the morning mist, like dew that goes early away. A faith that depends on social pressure evaporates the moment the pressure lifts, because it was mist all along. This is not a comfortable thought, but it is a clarifying one. Today, examine the supports under your own churchgoing and believing. How much of it is habit, how much is the comfort of belonging, how much is the fear of being thought strange. None of those are evil, but none of them are Christ, and a faith built on them is morning mist. Ask God to burn off the mist and leave what is real, even if what is left looks smaller than the crowd the culture used to gather for you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, much of what filled my pew was habit and fear and the comfort of belonging, and you see through all of it. Burn off the morning mist. Leave me the faith that is actually yours, however small it looks.

devotional.title: The Seed Is Still in the Ground
devotional.body: Grieve the right thing. Grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those, because they are good. But do not grieve the death of cultural Christianity as though the church were in the coffin. Jesus said unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies it bears much fruit. The whole gospel runs on that pattern. The seed must be buried to grow. The thing that looks like the end is the condition of the harvest. The church was born under a hostile empire with no laws on its side and no calendar in its favor, and it grew faster in those three centuries than in many of the comfortable ones after. It did not need Christendom to be born, and it will not need Christendom to survive its death. Today, let the loss become a planting rather than a funeral. Where you have been mourning the burial of an advantage, ask whether God is sowing a seed. The end of the arrangement that made faith convenient is not the end of the faith. It is the return of the church to the ground where it has always grown best. What dies is the empire's religion. What remains is the crucified man's church.
devotional.prayer: Lord of the buried seed, I have mourned a planting as if it were a funeral. Teach me to tell the death of an advantage from the death of the church. Grow your seed in the ground where you have buried it. Amen.

sessions.title: The Early Church Under Rome: Faith Without Power
sessions.aim: To study the three centuries the church grew with no army, no law, and no protection, and to ask whether we have any idea how to be that church again.
sessions.summary: Pliny the Younger did not know what to do with them, so around the year 112 he wrote the emperor asking how to handle the Christians he kept having to execute, not for any crime he could name but for the obstinacy itself, the flat refusal to do the small civic thing that would have saved them. That is the church we forget. For almost three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, the faith had no army, no friendly law, no social standing, and no guarantee that confessing the name would not cost a life. And it grew. Bell carries Paul's line written from inside the experience, afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, and notes the faith lived in that conjunction, in the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope. He steel-mans Rome, which was tolerant of religion and read the Christian refusal as sedition dressed as piety, a corrosive sect undermining a fragile civilization. Then he answers. The thing Rome read as corrosion was a different society planted inside the old one, a community that treated a slave and a senator as the same kind of creature, took in the infants Rome left to die, and nursed the sick during plagues when the healthy fled. Stark argued the church grew through plagues precisely because Christians stayed. When you cannot compel, you can only attract. See how they love one another was the only apologetic the empire could see. The blood of the martyrs was the seed, and it was the powerlessness that made the love legible.

keyScripture.why: Paul describes ordinary life under Rome as afflicted but not crushed, naming the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope.

discussion.q: Pliny executed Christians not for a crime he could name but for their refusal of one small civic gesture. Why was a pinch of incense worth dying over to them?
discussion.behind: Open on what the empire was actually asking. Rome rarely demanded a change of belief, only a gesture that signaled the state held your final loyalty. The Christians understood the gesture was the whole point. Help the room feel that the martyrs died over the one thing they had already given to Christ, the last word.

discussion.q: Bell points to Paul's grammar, afflicted but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed. What is the difference between not being crushed and winning, and why does it matter that we keep confusing them?
discussion.behind: You want them to separate survival of hope from victory of circumstance. The early church was not winning and was not crushed, and those are different claims. We have spent a long time pretending the second requires the first. Land it on the freedom of a faith that does not need to be winning to be alive.

discussion.q: Rome had real reasons to see the church as antisocial, a sect that would not absorb back into the civic religion. How do we take that seriously instead of treating the persecutors as cartoon villains?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness by honoring the empire's logic. If you believed the gods kept the harvest and the borders, a movement teaching people to insult them looked like a public danger. The point is not that Rome was simply evil but that the church offered a rival society, and that is what scandalized it.

discussion.q: Stark argued the church grew through plagues because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while others fled. What does it tell us that the faith spread fastest exactly when it had the least power?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal. When you cannot compel, you can only attract, and the attraction was bodies that stayed, tables where the wrong people ate together, infants taken in. Help them see that powerlessness made the love legible in a way power later hid. Tie it back to the camouflage of Christendom from session two.

discussion.q: Bell says he fears a future where the faith costs his sons something, but the early church was not afraid the way he is afraid. What are you most afraid of losing, and had the early church already lost it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The early church had already lost the safety and standing Bell is trying to protect, and found the losing did not touch what mattered. Invite people to name the thing they most fear losing and to ask whether the church Pliny could not explain had it at all.

objections.objection: Romanticizing persecution is easy from a comfortable pew. Suffering is not a strategy, and wishing the church back into the catacombs is a kind of spiritual tourism.
objections.response: Bell guards against exactly this by tracing the cost with dates and blood, Nero after the fire of 64, the martyrs of Lyon in 177, the empire-wide terror under Decius and Diocletian. He does not celebrate suffering. He notices that the church did its clearest work when it had no power, and warns that we should not assume we need the safety we are trying to protect. The point is not to chase martyrdom but to stop believing the faith cannot grow without an advantage it did without for three centuries.

objections.objection: If powerlessness is so holy, then Christians should stay out of public life entirely and let the world run itself while we tend our pure little community.
objections.response: That is the opposite overcorrection, and the early church refutes it. They did not withdraw into a private piety. They built a visible society inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues, and confronted the empire's idolatry to its face at the cost of their lives. Faith without power is not the same as faith without engagement. The church that attracts because it cannot compel is more public, not less, lived in the open where the world can see it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When have you been drawn to a community not by an argument it made but by the way it treated the people everyone else ignored?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing the early church was known for that requires no power and no platform. Stay with someone others are avoiding, care for a person the culture has written off, or quietly take responsibility for a need no law requires you to meet. Notice what it asks of you, and whether it feels like loss or like the church remembering its taste.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the church you grew had no army and no law and no place to stand, and it outlasted the empire that killed it. We have leaned so hard on safety and standing that we no longer know how to be the church without them. Take our fear of losing what Rome never gave the first Christians. Make our love legible the way theirs was, in bodies that stay when others flee. You had a tomb that would not stay shut. It was enough then. Let it be enough in us. Amen.
reflection: What would my faith look like if it could no longer compel anyone and could only attract, and would there be anything attractive left?
Where am I trusting the safety and standing the early church never had, and calling that trust faithfulness?
What is the small gesture I am unwilling to refuse, the incense I would burn to stay comfortable, and what does that reveal about my final loyalty?
sessions.teaching: Open with the puzzled governor, because Rome's confusion tells you what the church was. Around the year 112, Pliny the Younger wrote the emperor asking how to handle the Christians he kept having to execute. He had tried giving them three chances to curse Christ and worship the emperor's image. The stubborn ones he sent to die, not for any crime he could name, but for the obstinacy itself, the flat refusal to do the one small civic thing that would have saved them. Read that letter and you meet the early church the way Rome met it, not as a comfortable majority but as a problem to be managed by a bureaucrat with the power to kill. This is the church we forget. We picture cathedrals and councils and bishops who could write to kings as equals. But for almost three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, the church had no army, no friendly law, no social standing, and no guarantee that confessing the name would not cost a life. It was faith without power. And it grew. Carry Paul's sentence, written from inside the experience, not about it. We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed, perplexed, but not driven to despair, struck down, but not destroyed. The grammar matters. Afflicted but. Perplexed but. Struck down but. The faith lived in that conjunction, in the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope. They were not winning. They were not crushed. Those are different claims, and we have spent a long time pretending the second requires the first. Now steel-man the empire, because Rome was not a cartoon villain. Rome was tolerant of religion by ancient standards, absorbing gods the way it absorbed provinces. What it could not absorb was a group that refused to absorb back, that would not add the emperor to its shelf of gods and then declined the small sacrifice that signaled you were a safe member of society. From Rome's side this looked like sedition dressed as piety. If you believed the gods kept the harvest coming and the borders firm, a movement teaching people to insult them was a public danger. The persecutors, by their own lights, were defending the common good. So answer that. The thing Rome read as corrosion was the precise thing that made the church grow. The Christians did not grow by offering a better civic religion. They grew by offering what the empire structurally could not, a community that treated a slave and a senator as the same kind of creature, that took in the infants Rome exposed on the hillside to die, that nursed the sick during plagues when the healthy fled. Rodney Stark argued the church grew through plagues precisely because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while their neighbors ran, and the simple math of who survived and who was loved did the rest. The thing that looked antisocial to Rome was a different society planted inside the old one. Here is the engine of it. When you cannot compel, you can only attract. When you have no law to enforce your ethic, the ethic has to be lived in the open or it does not exist at all. See how they love one another was the only apologetic the empire could see. And there is a detail we rush past, so slow down. Rome rarely demanded that Christians stop believing. It demanded a gesture, a pinch of incense, the certificate proving you had sacrificed. The empire did not care what you held in your heart. It cared whether you would perform the public act that signaled your final loyalty belonged to the state. The Christians died over the gesture, because they understood the gesture was the whole point. It asked for the one thing they had already given to Christ, the place in the soul where only one Lord can sit. Here is the reversal, and it cuts toward us. We assume the church needs power to do its work. The first three centuries say the opposite. The church did its clearest work and grew at its fastest rate precisely when it had no power at all. It was the powerlessness that made the love legible. Once the church gained the empire, the love got harder to see, because now you could not tell who came for Christ and who came for Constantine.

scriptureStudy.note: Afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair. The Greek piles the pressure words against the rescue words. Paul is not describing victory. He is describing a hope the pressure cannot reach.
Persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. The conjunction but is the whole faith. The empire could do the first half to the body and could not touch the second half.
We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. The fragility is the point. The power is visible only because the vessel is plainly breakable.
Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that his life may be manifested. The cross is not an accident that befalls the church. It is the very means by which the life becomes visible.
By this all people will know you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. The only apologetic the empire could see was the love. When you cannot compel, the love is the whole argument.

scriptureStudy.ref: Tertullian, on the blood of the martyrs
scriptureStudy.note: Not Scripture but the church's own early reading of it, that the blood of the martyrs is the seed. The powerlessness made the witness legible in a way later power hid.

sessions.goingDeeper: Test the romance out of the persecution before you draw any lessons from it, because suffering is easy to admire from a safe pew. Trace the cost with dates, as the essay does. The persecution under Nero after the fire of 64. The martyrs of Lyon in 177, whom Eusebius records in unbearable detail. The empire-wide terror under Decius in 250, when every citizen had to produce a certificate proving they had sacrificed. The Great Persecution under Diocletian from 303, the last and worst. The advanced question is whether the growth came because of the suffering or despite it, and Rodney Stark's The Rise of Christianity offers a sociological answer that a careful group should weigh rather than simply accept. Stark argues the growth was driven less by martyrdom than by ordinary network conversion, higher birth rates, the refusal to expose infants, and the differential survival of Christians and those they nursed during the Antonine and Cyprianic plagues. Hold that honest complication. The witness of the martyrs was real, but the daily, unspectacular life of a different society may have done more demographic work than the executions. Then take up the harder theological question. If powerlessness made the love legible, is power therefore always a corruption, or did the church lose something real when it gained the means to build hospitals and schools at scale. A seminary group should resist both the triumphalism that reads Constantine as pure gain and the primitivism that reads the first three centuries as the only faithful church. The aim is to learn what faith without power knew, not to manufacture a persecution we do not have.
sessions.caseStudy: A sincere young man in your group has been reading about the early church and has come to a conclusion that worries you. He says the lesson is clear, that the church was pure when it stayed out of the world and got corrupted the moment it engaged, so the faithful thing now is to pull back, to build a small holy community, to stop wasting energy on the public square and the neighbors and the mess of the wider world, and just keep the church clean. He is not grasping for power. He is fleeing the world entirely, and calling the retreat holiness. His instinct against the power grab is right, and you should honor it. But the early church refutes his conclusion as firmly as it refutes the grab. They did not withdraw into a private piety. They built a visible society inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues when others fled, and confronted the empire's idolatry to its face at the cost of their lives. Faith without power was not the same as faith without engagement. The church that attracts because it cannot compel is more public, not less, lived in the open where the world can see it. Show him the door between his retreat and the church he admires. The early Christians were the most visible thing in the empire, not the most hidden.

memoryVerse.text: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed, perplexed, but not driven to despair, persecuted, but not forsaken, struck down, but not destroyed.

devotional.title: The Puzzled Governor
devotional.body: Around the year 112 a Roman governor named Pliny wrote his emperor, baffled, asking what to do with the Christians he kept executing. He could name no crime. They simply would not perform the small civic gesture that would have saved them, and they died for the obstinacy itself. Peter tells the church that if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name. The name itself was the offense. The Christians were not killed for a crime but for a loyalty, for reserving the deepest place in the soul for a Lord the empire could not control. We forget this church. We picture the faith with power and standing and a seat at the table, and we cannot imagine it as the thing a puzzled bureaucrat managed with executions. Today, sit with how strange the early Christians looked to Rome, and ask whether your own faith would have puzzled anyone. Is there anything in your believing that a watching outsider could not explain by ordinary self-interest, anything that would cost you something you could easily have kept. The early church was unmistakable. Ask God to make your faith legible in the same way, marked by a loyalty the world cannot account for.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the early church puzzled an empire with a loyalty it could not buy or break. Make my faith that legible. Let there be something in me a watching world cannot explain except by you.

devotional.title: Afflicted But Not Crushed
devotional.body: Paul described ordinary life under Rome with a string of conjunctions. Afflicted but not crushed. Perplexed but not driven to despair. Struck down but not destroyed. The whole faith lives in that little word but. It marks the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope. Notice what Paul does not claim. He does not say we are afflicted and winning, or struck down and prevailing. He says afflicted but not crushed, which is a smaller and a sturdier thing. They were not winning. They were not crushed. We have spent a long time pretending the second requires the first, that a faith not visibly triumphing must be failing. The early church knew better. Today, find the place in your life where you are afflicted, perplexed, struck down, and test whether you have confused not being crushed with winning. The promise is not that the pressure will lift or that your side will prevail. The promise is the conjunction, the but, the hope the pressure cannot reach. Ask God to let you live in that gap without demanding he close it, to be a person whose faith does not need to be winning in order to be alive.
devotional.prayer: Lord, teach me the strength of the small word but. When I am afflicted, perplexed, struck down, hold me in the gap your pressure cannot reach. Let me stop confusing not being crushed with winning.

devotional.title: When You Cannot Compel
devotional.body: When you cannot compel, you can only attract. The early church had no law to enforce its ethic, so the ethic had to be lived in the open or it did not exist at all. Jesus said the world would know his disciples by their love for one another, and for three centuries that was the only apologetic the empire could see. Not arguments it could not follow, but bodies that stayed when others fled, tables where the wrong people ate together, infants taken in that Rome had thrown away, the sick nursed during plagues when the healthy ran. The love was legible precisely because the church had no power to hide behind. Today, ask what your faith looks like when it cannot compel anyone. Strip away every lever, every social pressure, every advantage, and what is left that would still attract a watching neighbor. The honest answer for many of us is uncomfortable, because we have leaned so long on the culture doing the work that we are not sure the love is there underneath. Do one thing today that requires no power and no platform, one act of love the world cannot explain and does not reward. See whether your faith can still attract when it can no longer compel.
devotional.prayer: Lord, when I cannot compel anyone, let me attract them the way the early church did, by a love that needs no power to be real. Strip away my levers and leave the love that draws people to you.

devotional.title: The Pinch of Incense
devotional.body: Rome rarely asked Christians to stop believing. It asked for a gesture, a pinch of incense on the altar, a few words acknowledging the emperor. The belief could be kept privately if only the body would bow publicly. To a Roman it looked insane to die over so small a thing. But the early church understood the gesture was the whole point. It asked for the one thing they had already given to Christ, the last word, the place in the soul where only one Lord can sit. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego stood before a furnace and told the king their God was able to deliver them, but if not, they still would not bow. But if not. That is the faith that will not burn the incense. It does not bargain on rescue. It simply will not give the gesture that signals another lord holds the final loyalty. Today, find the pinch of incense in your own life, the small gesture you are willing to make to stay comfortable, the bow that looks like nothing and gives away everything. It may be a silence you keep, a loyalty you perform, a compromise you call prudence. Ask God for the courage of the three men before the furnace, who would not bow even if he did not save them.
devotional.prayer: Lord, show me the pinch of incense I keep burning to stay safe, the small bow that gives away the last word. Give me the courage of the three before the furnace. Let me say, but if not, I still will not bow.

devotional.title: A Tomb That Would Not Stay Shut
devotional.body: They had no power. They had a tomb that would not stay shut, and it was enough to outlast Rome. Luke says the apostles gave their witness to the resurrection with great power, and great grace was upon them all, and the power was not an army or a law or a seat at the table. It was an empty grave and a love the empire could not produce. I think about my sons inheriting a country where the faith costs something again, and part of me fears it. But the church I read about in those three centuries was not afraid the way I am afraid. It had already lost the safety and standing I am trying to protect, and it found that the losing did not touch the only thing that mattered. End the week by naming what you most fear losing, the safety, the standing, the advantage, and asking whether the early church had it at all. They did without it for three hundred years and grew anyway, because they were not trusting the things you are trying to keep. Ask God to take your fear of losing what Rome never gave the first Christians, and to make the empty tomb enough for you the way it was enough for them. They had no power. They had a Lord who walked out of a grave. It was enough then. Let it be enough now.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the early church had no power and an empty tomb, and the tomb was enough to outlast an empire. Take my fear of losing what those first Christians never had. Let the risen Christ be enough in me. Amen.

sessions.title: Two Kingdoms: How Christians Relate Faith and State
sessions.aim: To recover the two-kingdoms teaching as a discipline that holds a tension, honoring the office while judging the officeholder, rather than a wall that silences the church or a license that baptizes the state.
sessions.summary: A man asked Bell once whether a Christian should care about politics, and behind the question were two opposite fears, that the church had become a wing of a party, and that answering no would abandon the poor and the unborn and the prisoner. Both fears are right, and the old language of two kingdoms was built to hold them. The phrase means roughly that God rules the world in two ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross, and through the civil order by law and the sword, and that these are not the same rule and must not collapse into each other. It has been abused in both directions, used to tell the church to stay out of public life entirely and used to let the state do whatever it wants. Bell carries the most misused text, let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and shows Paul wrote it to a church the empire would soon burn, not as a blank check but with a leash, since the authority is a servant given a defined job, and a job defined is a job that can be failed. He steel-mans the strongest separation, which is wisdom paid for in blood, the crusade and the inquisition and the wars of religion. Augustine answered from inside the tradition with two cities mingled in history, distinguishable by their loves, telling Christians to seek the city's peace without confusing it with home. The cross is the line. It tells the church it does not rule by force and tells the state it does not rule by right of heaven. The German church learned the cost of forgetting, and Barmen answered that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word we must obey. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second clause and you have lost the point.

keyScripture.why: Paul commands submission to the authorities and in the same passage defines their job as God's servants for good, so the text that demands submission is the text that lets us judge a state that fails it.

discussion.q: Bell says the man who asked whether Christians should care about politics carried two opposite fears at once. Which of those two fears do you feel more strongly, and why?
discussion.behind: Open by getting both fears into the room, the church as a party wing and the church abandoning the vulnerable. The point is that both are legitimate, and the two-kingdoms teaching exists to hold them together. Notice which fear the room leans toward, because that reveals which abuse it is most likely to commit.

discussion.q: Romans 13 commands submission, but Bell shows the same passage defines the authority's job as a servant for good. How does a job defined become a job that can be failed?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The text used to bless tyrants for two thousand years is the same text that puts the state on a leash. If the authority is God's servant with a defined task, the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. Help them feel that submission and judgment live in the same verse.

discussion.q: Bell honors the strongest case for keeping the kingdoms separate as wisdom paid for in blood, the crusade, the inquisition, the religious wars. What is that separation rightly guarding against?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness by honoring the separation before complicating it. A church that holds the sword stops persuading and starts coercing, and a state that claims divine sanction becomes a god with an army. Make sure the room sees the separation as hard-won wisdom, not cowardice, before the reversal.

discussion.q: Bell says the German church in the 1930s turned two kingdoms into two sealed rooms, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. How does the doctrine done right do the opposite of silencing the church?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal, and it is the center of the session. Two kingdoms rightly understood does not free the state from judgment, it subjects the state to a higher court and gives the church a place to stand outside it. Only a church that knows it is a different kingdom can tell Caesar he is not God. Barmen is the model.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has watched pastors trade the prophetic voice for a seat at the table, whichever party's table, and call it courage. Where have you seen, or felt in yourself, a faith so fused to a program that it could no longer rebuke it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, leader first, and keep it pointed in every direction. The chaplain who cannot rebuke the power he loves comes in a conservative and a progressive version. Invite honest naming of where each person has let a political loyalty silence the word they should have spoken. Go first if needed.

objections.objection: Two kingdoms is just a clever way to tell the church to shut up and stay in its lane while the state does as it pleases. It silences the prophets.
objections.response: That is the abuse Bell names directly, the German error of two sealed rooms, and the doctrine done right reverses it. If the state is God's servant with a defined job, the church is the very body that can say when the servant has failed. The separation is not a wall protecting the state from the church's voice. It is the vantage point from which the church can tell Caesar he is not God. A church that knows it is a different kingdom is the only one that can prophesy to this one.

objections.objection: If the church really believes the gospel, it should pick up the state's power and use it to make the country righteous. Why leave the sword to the unbelievers?
objections.response: Bell rules this out at the cross. The church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it, told Peter to put it away, and conquered by being conquered. A gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. The two-kingdoms discipline is not passivity. It is serving the city, paying the tax, honoring the office, while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King, so that when the city asks to be worshiped as a god, the church has somewhere to stand and the words to refuse.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a political power you love so much that you would find it hard to rebuke it even when it was clearly wrong?
sessions.practice: This week, find one place where you have fused the gospel with a political program until you can no longer tell them apart. Practice honoring the office while judging the officeholder, naming one thing your own side has done that the cross condemns. Notice whether you can still see the seam between your faith and your party, and write down what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you rule the church by the word and the world by the sword, and you are the one Lord over both. We have collapsed the two into one, sometimes silencing your church to keep the peace, sometimes seizing the state to win. Forgive us for the tables we sold our prophetic voice to sit at. Let us serve the city and pay the tax and honor the office, and keep one foot planted with the crucified King, so that when the city asks us to bow, we have somewhere to stand. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Hold us to the second clause. Amen.
reflection: Which abuse am I more tempted toward, a church that grabs the state's sword or a church that goes silent before it, and why that one?
Where have I so identified the gospel with a political program that I can no longer rebuke the power I love?
Do I honor the office while still judging the officeholder, or have I let my loyalty to a side decide in advance what I am willing to call wrong?
sessions.teaching: Begin with the man and his two fears, because both are right and the doctrine exists to hold them. A man asked me once whether a Christian should care about politics, and behind his question were two opposite fears. He was afraid the church had become a wing of a party, praying in the colors of a campaign. He was also afraid that answering no would mean abandoning the poor and the unborn and the prisoner to whatever the powerful decided. Both fears are right, and that is what the old language of two kingdoms was built to hold. The phrase means roughly this, that God rules the world in two ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross, and through the civil order by law and the sword, and these are not the same rule and must not collapse into each other. Like every old idea it has been abused in both directions, used to tell the church to stay out of public life entirely, and used to let the state do whatever it wants. Neither is what the teaching was for. Carry the text everyone reaches for and few read whole. Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God. That sentence has blessed tyrants for two thousand years. But Paul wrote it to a church in the capital of an empire that would, within a decade, burn his own people in Nero's gardens, and he wrote it not as a blank check but with a leash. The authority is a servant of God, a terror to bad conduct and not to good. The state is given a job, and the text that commands submission is the same text that defines the job, and a job defined is a job that can be failed. Steel-man the strongest version of the separation, because it is not cowardice, it is wisdom paid for in blood. The people who most want faith and state kept distinct have often read the most history. They know what happened when the church held the sword, the crusade and the inquisition and the wars of religion that turned Europe into a charnel house.
