They know a church with state power stops persuading and starts coercing, and that a gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. They are not telling the church to be silent. They are telling it not to pick up the sword. So answer that from inside the tradition. Augustine wrote The City of God after Rome fell in 410, describing two cities, one built on love of God and one on love of self, mingled in history until the end, distinguishable by their loves. He did not tell Christians to abandon the earthly city. He told them to use it, seek its peace, serve it, while never confusing it with home. You can love your country hard and still know it is not your King. Here the cross does its work against both abuses at once. A church that grabs the state's sword forgets its Lord refused the sword and told Peter to put it away. And a state that claims the church's authority forgets that the only throne the church recognizes is occupied by a man Rome executed. Stand at the cross and you cannot baptize the sword and you cannot silence the church. Trace the failure, because the doctrine has a graveyard. In the 1930s a strand of two-kingdoms thinking had decayed into a tidy division of labor, the church handling the soul, the state handling the body, the church with no business judging what the state did in its own sphere. That decayed doctrine helped a church stay quiet while a regime did what it did. The Confessing Church declared at Barmen in 1934 that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word of God we must obey, that there are no areas of life where we belong to another lord. Two kingdoms had become two sealed rooms, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. Here is the reversal. People reach for two kingdoms to get the church out of politics, but the doctrine done right does the opposite. It does not free the state from judgment. It subjects the state to a higher court. If the governing authority is God's servant with a defined job, then the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. Only the church that knows it is a different kingdom can tell Caesar he is not God. Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second clause and you have lost the point.

scriptureStudy.note: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. Read it whole and in its setting, written to Christians in Nero's Rome. It is a command to submit, and the very next verses turn it into a leash.

Rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. The authority is given a defined purpose. The moment a ruler becomes a terror to the good and a friend to the bad, he has stepped outside the job this text assigns him.

He is God's servant for your good, the word is diakonos, a servant under orders. A servant has a master and a task, and a servant can be unfaithful. The text that demands submission is the text that defines failure.

Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by it. The Lord of the church refused the sword at his own arrest. A church that grabs the state's sword has forgotten its King in the garden.

We must obey God rather than men. Submission to the authorities is real but not absolute. When the servant commands what the master forbids, the higher loyalty governs, and the church has somewhere to stand.

The same Rome that Romans 13 calls God's servant, Revelation 13 draws as a beast demanding worship. Hold both. The authority that serves God can become the authority that plays God, and Scripture names both faces.

sessions.goingDeeper: Work the history of the doctrine so the room does not flatten it into a slogan. The two-kingdoms language runs through Augustine's two cities, takes sharp form in Luther's distinction between the kingdom of God's right hand and his left, and develops differently again in the Reformed and Anabaptist traditions, each protecting against a different danger and each abusable in a different way. The Lutheran version, in the wrong hands, can decay into the quietism that sealed the German church, the conviction that the gospel governs the soul while the state governs the world without spiritual accountability. The theocratic temptation runs the opposite way, collapsing the two kingdoms into one so the church wields the sword directly. A careful group should locate where each tradition guards the gospel and where each can be bent to excuse either passivity or coercion. Bring in the Barmen Declaration of 1934 as the decisive modern test, and read its first thesis closely, that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God we have to hear and obey in life and death, and that the church rejects the false doctrine that there are areas of life belonging to other lords. Set Bonhoeffer's Ethics beside it, his break with a two-kingdoms thinking decayed into two sealed rooms, written from inside the failure. The seminary-trained group should weigh whether Barmen abolishes the two kingdoms or rescues them, and notice that the answer Bell gives is the second. The distinction is not a wall that silences the church. It is the vantage from which the church can tell the state it is not God.
sessions.caseStudy: An energetic newer believer in your group is impatient with all this talk of tension and restraint. He says the country is sliding into evil while Christians sit on their hands, that God has given the church the truth and the votes to fix it, and that the faithful thing is to take power, capture the courts and the legislatures and the schools, and use the state to make the nation righteous by law. Why, he asks, would we leave the sword to the unbelievers. He is not retreating. He wants the throne, and he is sure that wanting it is courage. His zeal for righteousness is real, and his frustration with a passive church is not wrong, and you should honor both before you complicate them. But the cross rules out his plan. The church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it, told Peter to put it away, and conquered by being conquered. A gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. Show him that the two-kingdoms discipline is not the passivity he despises. It is serving the city, honoring the office, working hard for justice, while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King, so that when the state asks to be worshiped, the church has somewhere to stand and the words to refuse. The sword he wants would cost him the gospel he means to defend.

devotional.title: Two Fears at Once
devotional.body: A man asked me whether a Christian should care about politics, and behind his question were two opposite fears. He feared the church had become a wing of a party, praying in the colors of a campaign. He also feared that answering no would mean abandoning the poor and the unborn and the prisoner to whatever the powerful decided. Both fears are right. Micah names what the Lord requires, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God. Hold the three together and you see why the man was torn. Do justice pushes the church toward the public square and the cause of the vulnerable. Walk humbly pulls it back from the arrogance of seizing power to enforce its will. The faithful life lives in the tension between them, not in the collapse of one into the other. Today, notice which of the two fears you feel more strongly, because that reveals which error you are more likely to commit. If you fear the church grabbing power, you may be tempted to silence it. If you fear the church going passive, you may be tempted to make it a party. Ask God for the harder thing, a heart that can do justice and walk humbly at once, refusing both the chaplain's silence and the crusader's sword.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you ask me to do justice and to walk humbly, and I am tempted to drop one to hold the other. Hold me in the tension. Keep me from the silence that abandons and the power that corrupts.

devotional.title: A Leash, Not a Blank Check
devotional.body: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. The sentence has blessed tyrants for two thousand years, quoted by every ruler who wanted obedience without accountability. But read it whole. Paul wrote it to Christians in the capital of an empire that would soon burn them, and he wrote it not as a blank check but with a leash. The authority is God's servant, Paul says, for your good, a terror to bad conduct and not to good. The state is given a job. And the text that commands submission is the same text that defines the job, which means a job defined is a job that can be failed. Today, hold both halves of the verse together, because most people hold only one. Some quote the command to submit and forget the defined purpose, blessing whatever the powerful do. Others reject the command to submit and forget that honoring the office is also commanded. The faithful reading keeps both. Honor the office. Pay the tax. Submit to the authority. And remember that the same God who appointed the servant defined his task, so the church may say, without rebellion, when the servant has betrayed the master. Submission and judgment live in the same verse. Ask God to let you hold them both.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you command me to honor the authorities and you also define their task. Let me submit without worshiping and judge without rebelling. Help me hold the whole verse, the leash and the command together.

devotional.title: Two Cities, One Age
devotional.body: Augustine wrote The City of God after Rome fell, when pagans blamed the Christians for the collapse. He described two cities, one built on love of God and one on love of self, mingled together in this age, distinguishable not by their borders but by their loves. He did not tell Christians to flee the earthly city. He told them to use it, to seek its peace, to serve it, while never confusing it with home. Jeremiah said the same to the exiles in Babylon. Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray for it, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. Love the city. Serve it. Pray for it. And never mistake it for the kingdom of God. Today, practice the citizenship of the two cities. Work for the good of the actual place you live, its peace and its poor and its order, with real energy and without apology. But hold it loosely enough to remember it is not your home and not your King. The Christian who only serves the city has forgotten he is an exile. The Christian who only despises the city has forgotten he was sent there. Walk the line Augustine walked, serving the earthly city hard while keeping his heart in the city of God. You can love your country with everything and still know it is not your King.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you sent me into a city that is not my home and told me to seek its welfare. Let me serve it hard and love it well, and never mistake it for the kingdom. Keep my heart in the city of God.

devotional.title: The Sword in the Garden
devotional.body: When the soldiers came to arrest Jesus, Peter drew a sword and struck, and Jesus told him to put it back, for all who take the sword will perish by it. The Lord of the church refused the sword at the very moment it seemed most justified, when they came to take him to a cross. This is the line the church keeps forgetting. A church that grabs the state's sword to enforce the gospel has forgotten its King in the garden, who could have called twelve legions of angels and called none. A gospel advanced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel, because the gospel is the news about a man who conquered by being conquered. Today, examine where you have reached for Peter's sword in your own heart, where you have believed the cause of Christ depends on your seizing some power, winning some fight, forcing some outcome. The instinct feels like courage. Jesus called it a misunderstanding of his kingdom. Lay the sword down. Not because justice does not matter, but because the kingdom does not come by the sword and never has. Ask God to show you the difference between contending for what is right and grasping for the power to compel it, and to give you the strange courage of the King who would not let his servants fight.
devotional.prayer: Jesus, you refused the sword in the garden when it seemed most justified, and I keep reaching for it in your name. Show me where I have grasped for power and called it courage. Teach me to put the sword back.

devotional.title: One Word We Must Obey
devotional.body: In 1934 the Confessing Church declared at Barmen that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word of God we must obey, that there are no areas of life where we belong to another lord. They said it because a church had let two kingdoms become two sealed rooms, the gospel for the soul and the state for everything else, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. The apostles had said it first, before the council that forbade them to preach. We must obey God rather than men. This is the second clause the church forgets. Two kingdoms, one Lord. The distinction between the kingdoms was never a wall to silence the church before the state. It was the vantage from which the church could tell the state it is not God. End the week here. Ask whether you have let your faith become a sealed room, private and harmless, kept carefully out of the rooms where the real decisions are made. Or whether, in the other direction, you have fused your faith so tightly to a political program that it could no longer rebuke the power it loves. Both forget the one Lord over both kingdoms. Ask God to give you a faith that serves the state without worshiping it and judges the state without seizing it, that knows one Word, and obeys it, in every room.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you are the one Word over both kingdoms, and I keep forgetting the second clause. Free me from the sealed room and from the fused one. Let me serve the state and never bow to it, and obey you in every room. Amen.

sessions.title: The Church After Cultural Power
sessions.aim: To face that the church no longer sets the terms of the culture and to ask the harder question, whether it ever knew how to be the church without them.
sessions.summary: The store stayed closed on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God, and now it does not, and a certain kind of Christian experiences that as the world ending. Bell grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free, the calendar and the schools and the social pressure all leaning the way the sermon did. That arrangement is gone, and the real question is not how to get the terms back but whether the church ever knew how to be the church without them. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is the loss of advantage. Strip away the home-field edge and attendance falls, partly because the people who never really believed stopped pretending. Bell carries the salt saying, and reads the warning we skip, that salt works by being different from the dish, and the danger is not that the world overpowers it but that it dissolves until no one can taste the difference. He steel-mans the grief, which is love looking at a wound, since real goods eroded when the culture stopped honoring the faith. Then he answers. The church protected those goods by borrowing the state's machinery rather than by being the church, mistaking a borrowed majority for its own strength, learning to win by counting votes instead of making disciples. A victory won that way cannot be kept. The cross exposes what we trusted, because a crucified Lord refutes the idea that the kingdom advances by holding the levers. The end of cultural Christianity is a test of whether anything is left when the advantage is gone, mercy disguised as decline. The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it.

keyScripture.why: Jesus warns that salt loses its use not when the world overpowers it but when it dissolves until no one can taste the difference, which is what Christendom tempted the church to do.

discussion.q: Bell says much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is really the loss of advantage. Where, honestly, do you feel the difference between grieving Christ and grieving the home-field edge?
discussion.behind: Open on the hardest claim of the session, said gently. The decline is partly a subtraction of the nominal and the convenient, people who never believed no longer pretending. Help the room separate the loss of the faith from the loss of the cultural support, without dismissing the genuine pain in either.

discussion.q: The salt warning is not that the world overpowers the salt but that the salt dissolves until no one can taste it. How was Christendom a long temptation to dissolve?
discussion.behind: You want them to see that the danger was never hostility but sameness. We added ourselves so thoroughly to the culture that no one could taste the difference, voting the same fears, chasing the same security. Tie this back to the camouflage from sessions two and three. Salt does its work by not dissolving.

discussion.q: Bell honors the grief as love looking at a wound, naming real goods that eroded when the culture stopped honoring the faith. How do we take that grief seriously and still ask the harder question?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The people mourning lost cultural power are often mourning the unborn, the poor, the support around marriage, real things the gospel cares about. Make sure no one feels their grief is being mocked before the harder point lands, that the goods were held by borrowed power rather than converted hearts.

discussion.q: Bell says the church learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way cannot be kept. Why is a borrowed majority weaker than it looks?
discussion.behind: This is the reversal. A consensus held by cultural habit is always one election from collapse because it rests on power rather than persuaded hearts. The church mistook the home-field edge for its own strength and could not tell how weak it was. Help them feel why formation is slower but sturdier than legislation.

discussion.q: Bell describes two responses to the loss, one fighting to recapture the levers and one quietly building communities so distinct a neighbor has to ask what makes them that way. Which response is more natural to you, and which do you want to hand the next generation?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and a real choice, leader first. Bell is not neutral, and neither are you, but invite honesty rather than performance. The first response has a louder voice and a worse record. The second looks like the people Pliny could not explain. Let people name which one they have actually been living.

objections.objection: So the answer is for Christians to retreat into pure little communities and give up on the public square, abandoning the vulnerable to whoever stays in the fight.
objections.response: Bell rules out the retreat as firmly as he rules out the panic. The community he points to is not a bunker, it is a society so distinct that the watching world is drawn to it, the kind that takes in the discarded and forms people who live differently in public. The early church had no cultural power and was not withdrawn, it was the most visible thing in the empire. Losing the levers is not the same as leaving the world. It is finding out whether the church can be salt without the wind at its back.

objections.objection: If Christendom protected the unborn and the poor and marriage, then losing it is a disaster, and the faithful thing is to fight to get the cultural power back.
objections.response: Grant the wound fully, because those goods were real and Bell says fight for them. The question he presses is how the church held them, by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery of compulsion. A protection that rests on a majority rather than on converted hearts is always one election from collapse, and the church mistook that borrowed strength for its own. The deeper work is forming a people who would live the mercy when the law no longer requires it, which is the only kind of strength the early church ever had.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the culture stopped doing any of the church's work for you tomorrow, what part of your faith would simply stop, and what would keep going?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing that makes you distinct rather than blended, one act of mercy or honesty or generosity that the surrounding culture cannot explain and does not reward. Do not announce it. Just notice whether your faith can act on its own, without the wind of approval at its back, and write down what you learn about your own saltiness.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, the culture is done carrying us, and we are afraid, because we have leaned on it so long we are not sure what is left underneath. Forgive us for trusting the levers more than the cross, for winning by counting votes when you called us to make disciples. Strip away the camouflage. Make us salt that remembers its taste, a people so marked by you that a watching neighbor has to ask what makes us this way. You grew your church with every cultural lever pulling the other way. Do it again in us. Amen.
reflection: How much of my religion is power and advantage, and how much of my witness could survive without the wind at my back?
Have I been fighting to recapture the levers or building a community distinct enough to be noticed, and which one have I called faithfulness?
When the culture stops doing the church's work, what will be left of my faith, and does that answer comfort me or frighten me?
sessions.teaching: Start at the closed store, because that is where the grief lives. The store stayed closed on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God, and now it does not, and a certain kind of Christian experiences that as the world ending. I understand the feeling. I grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free, where the calendar and the schools and the social pressure all leaned the way the sermon did. That arrangement is gone. The church no longer sets the terms. The real question is not how to get the terms back. It is whether the church ever knew how to be the church without them. This is the hard part to say to grieving people. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is the loss of advantage. We had a home-field edge for a long time, the assumption that decent and Christian were near synonyms, the social cost attached to leaving rather than staying. Strip that away and attendance falls, not because people stopped believing so much as because those who never really believed stopped pretending. The decline is partly a subtraction of the nominal and the convenient. It hurts, and it is also a kind of honesty arriving late. Carry the salt saying, and read the warning we skip. You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored, it is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled. We read the first clause as a compliment and skip the warning, which is the whole point. Salt works by being different from the dish, by not dissolving. The danger Jesus names is not that the world will overpower the salt. It is that the salt will become indistinguishable from what surrounds it, and then be good for nothing. Christendom was the long temptation to dissolve. We added ourselves so thoroughly to the culture that no one could taste the difference anymore. Steel-man the grief, because it is not foolish. The people who mourn the church's lost cultural power are often mourning real losses with real names. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn had more protection, the poor had more institutions tending them, marriage had more support around it. Those were goods, and a flippant Christianity that celebrates their loss as freedom has stopped loving its neighbors. That grief is not weakness. It is love looking at a wound. So answer the strong version. Yes, those were goods, and their erosion is a real wound. But the question is whether the church protected them by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery of compulsion, and the difference is everything. When the unborn were protected by a cultural consensus rather than by a converted people, the protection was always one election from collapse, because it rested on power rather than on persuaded hearts. The church mistook a borrowed majority for its own strength. It learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way cannot be kept. The cross does the work here by exposing what we actually trusted. A crucified Lord is the permanent refutation of the idea that the kingdom advances by holding the levers. Jesus held no levers. He had no majority, no favorable law, and the consensus he did encounter voted to kill him. The church that grieves its lost power is, without meaning to, confessing that it had started to trust the levers more than the cross. Here is the reversal, and I include myself in it. We say we want the culture back so we can serve our neighbors better, and some of that is true. But some of it is that the loss of power has exposed how much of our religion was power, how little of our witness could survive without the wind at our back. The end of cultural Christianity is a test, and the test is whether anything is left when the advantage is gone. I have watched congregations respond in two ways. Some grow frightened and pour their energy into recapturing the levers. Others, quieter, stop waiting for the culture to do their work and start doing it themselves, forming people, taking in the discarded, building communities so distinct that a neighbor has to ask what makes them that way. The first looks like fighting to restore Christendom. The second looks like the people Pliny could not explain. The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it.

scriptureStudy.note: You are the salt of the earth. The compliment we love. But salt exists to be different from the dish, to season and preserve by not blending in. The identity is inseparable from the distinctness.

If salt has lost its taste, how shall it be restored. The danger is not that the world overpowers the salt but that the salt dissolves until no one can taste it. Christendom was the long temptation to dissolve.
It is no longer good for anything but to be thrown out and trampled. The trampling does not come from the world's hostility. It comes from the salt forgetting what it was for and becoming the dish.
A city on a hill, a lamp on a stand. The witness is meant to be visible and distinct, not hidden and not blended. Salt and light both work by being unmistakably other than their surroundings.

The word of the cross is folly to those perishing but the power of God to us. The kingdom's power is the cross, not the lever. A church that trusts the lever has confessed it no longer believes the word of the cross can do anything.
Our citizenship is in heaven. The post-Christendom church relearns the exile's posture, distinct and resident, serving the city without mistaking it for home, salt that remembers its taste.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press the diagnosis past the easy version. James Davison Hunter in To Change the World argues that the church's dominant strategies for cultural influence, the political conquest of the right and the social-justice activism of the left alike, share a flawed theory of how cultures actually change, an overconfidence in politics and ideas and a blindness to the slow work of institutions and networks. His alternative, faithful presence, is worth weighing against the essay's instinct, and a careful group should ask whether Bell's distinct community and Hunter's faithful presence are the same proposal or differ in important ways. Set this beside William Cavanaugh's critique that the modern church too readily accepts the role the state assigns it, a private provider of values to prop up the public order, forgetting that it is itself a public, a body politic with its own way of life. The advanced question is whether the loss of cultural power is best read as catastrophe, opportunity, or judgment, and the most honest answer may be all three at once. Then take up the hardest counterpoint the essay invites. If the cultural consensus genuinely protected the vulnerable, is it not a real harm to lose it, and is the call to slow formation a way of accepting that harm too lightly. A seminary group should resist the temptation to romanticize powerlessness, just as session three warned, and weigh whether faithful presence can in fact protect the vulnerable or whether it quietly cedes the field. Bell refuses both the panic and the retreat. The work is to locate where that refusal actually stands and whether it can hold weight.
sessions.caseStudy: A capable woman in your group, once active in every ministry, has gone quiet and a little bitter. When you reach the question about the two responses, she says she is done. She fought the culture wars for twenty years, manned the phone banks, marched, voted, and lost, and now she has decided the world is going to do what it wants and the only sane move is to tend her own garden, raise her kids, and stop caring what happens out there. She is not grasping for the levers. She has dropped them entirely and called the despair peace. Her exhaustion is real and you should honor it, because she has carried more than most and the loss is genuine. But notice that her retreat is the mirror of the recapture she abandoned, and the early church refutes both. The community Bell points to is not a bunker. It is a society so distinct that the watching world is drawn to it, that takes in the discarded and forms people who live differently in public. Losing the levers is not the same as leaving the world. Show her gently that the alternative to the culture war was never the walled garden. It was salt, lived in the open, visible enough that a neighbor has to ask. Her withdrawal is not the rest she thinks it is. It is the salt deciding to stop being salt.

memoryVerse.text: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet.

devotional.title: The Loss of Advantage
devotional.body: Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is the loss of advantage. We had a home-field edge for a long time, the assumption that decent and Christian were near synonyms, the social cost attached to leaving rather than staying. Strip that away and attendance falls, partly because the people who never really believed stopped pretending. Jesus warned that salt which loses its taste is fit for nothing and is thrown out. He did not say the world would defeat the salt. He said the salt could lose the very thing that made it salt. This is the uncomfortable clarity in the decline. Some of what is falling away was never faith at all. It was habit, respectability, the convenience of belonging. Today, separate in your own heart the loss of Christ from the loss of the cultural edge. When you feel the grief of a changing country, ask honestly which one you are mourning. There is real loss to grieve, and there is the mere subtraction of an advantage that was never the gospel. Telling them apart is not cold. It is the beginning of honesty about where your faith was actually resting. Ask God to show you how much of what you call faith was wind at your back, and whether the thing underneath could fly without it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have mourned the loss of an advantage as though it were the loss of you. Show me the difference. Strip away what was only habit and comfort, and let me find what is actually faith underneath.

devotional.title: Salt That Dissolves
devotional.body: The salt does not lose its use because the world overpowers it. It loses its use by dissolving into the dish until no one can taste the difference. That was the long temptation of Christendom. We added ourselves so thoroughly to the culture that no one could taste anything distinct, voting the same fears, chasing the same security, divorcing at the same rate, the only visible difference an hour on Sunday. Paul says do not be conformed to this world but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Conformity is the dissolving. It is the salt becoming the dish. The danger to the church has rarely been open hostility. It has been sameness, the slow blending in that leaves nothing for a watching world to taste. Today, look for the places where you have dissolved, where your life is indistinguishable from your neighbor's who confesses nothing. What do you fear, and is it the same thing everyone fears. What do you chase, and is it the same thing everyone chases. Salt does its work by staying salt, by not blending all the way in. Ask God to make you distinct again, not strange for its own sake, but unmistakably seasoned by a different hope, so that someone tasting your life would notice a flavor the culture cannot produce.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have dissolved into the dish until no one can taste the difference. Forgive my conformity. Renew my mind and make me salt again, distinct enough to season, different enough to be noticed.

devotional.title: Love Looking at a Wound
devotional.body: The grief is not foolish, and we should not pretend it is. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn had more protection, the poor had more institutions tending them, marriage had more support around it. Those were goods, and to celebrate their loss as freedom is to stop loving your neighbor. Proverbs says open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute, defend the poor and the needy. The believer who grieves the erosion of these protections is often grieving exactly what the gospel cares about. That grief is not weakness. It is love looking at a wound. Today, do not let any clever theology numb you to real losses. If institutions that protected the vulnerable have weakened, that is a wound worth grieving and worth working to heal. The point of distinguishing love of country from worship of it, advantage from faith, was never to make you indifferent to your neighbor's suffering. It was to free you to love your neighbor without needing to control the culture first. Hold your grief honestly. Then ask the harder question the grief invites. Were those goods held by converted hearts or by borrowed power, and which one can actually last.
devotional.prayer: Lord, let me grieve the real wounds without numbing my heart with easy answers. Open my mouth for the voiceless and my hands for the poor. Let my love look honestly at the wound and still work to heal it.

devotional.title: A Borrowed Majority
devotional.body: Here is the hard truth under the grief. When the unborn or the poor were protected by a cultural consensus rather than by a converted people, the protection was always one election from collapse, because it rested on power rather than on persuaded hearts. The church learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way cannot be kept. Zechariah heard the word of the Lord, not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. The church mistook a borrowed majority for its own strength and could not tell how weak it was, because the home-field edge hid the weakness. Formation is slower than legislation, but it is sturdier, because a person formed to live the mercy will live it when the law no longer requires it, and a majority will not. Today, examine where you have trusted might and power, the vote, the law, the cultural pressure, to do what only the Spirit does through changed hearts. The work of the Spirit is slower and quieter and looks weaker, and it is the only kind of strength that lasts. Ask God to free you from the anxiety of the borrowed majority, and to give you the patience to make disciples rather than only to count votes, even when discipleship looks like losing.
devotional.prayer: Lord, not by might nor by power but by your Spirit. Forgive me for trusting the borrowed majority and calling it strength. Give me patience for the slow work of formation, the only strength that lasts.

devotional.title: Now We Find Out
devotional.body: The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it. The loss of power has exposed how much of our religion was power, how little of our witness could survive without the wind at our back. A church that could only be the church when the culture agreed with it was never depending on the Spirit. It was depending on the culture. Peter says it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God, and this judgment is mercy disguised as decline. It is the test of whether anything is left when the advantage is gone. There were two responses around me, and they revealed everything. Some grew frightened and poured their energy into recapturing the levers. Others, quieter, stopped waiting for the culture to do their work and started building communities so distinct that a neighbor had to ask what made them that way. The first has a louder voice and a worse record. The second looks like the people Pliny could not explain. End the week with the real choice. Which response have you been living, and which do you want to hand the next generation. Do not flee the world and do not grasp for its levers. Be salt, in the open, distinct enough to be tasted. The culture will not carry you anymore. Find out whether you believed it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the culture is done carrying me, and now I find out what was faith and what was only power. Let the test be mercy. Make me salt that remembers its taste, distinct enough that someone has to ask what makes me this way. Amen.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the dates and the names. It is settling your own heart. The aim of this series is narrow and it is hard. It is to recover how the church relates to political power, from a coin held up in a trap to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default of the West, and to keep the crucified King above every throne in a room full of people who arrived with that order already scrambled in different directions. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to win an argument. It is not to move people to the left or the right. It is not to produce a room that finally agrees with you. If anyone leaves voting differently but loving Christ no more than before, the study failed, no matter how satisfying the conversion felt. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face is the temptation to turn this into a political brawl, and that temptation will not announce itself as a brawl. It will arrive dressed as truth-telling, as finally saying the thing that needs saying, as the righteous heat of being right. Refuse it. The moment the room splits into a side that is winning and a side that is losing, the study has stopped doing its work, because its work was to indict every tribe, including yours and including mine. The whole series is built to catch two opposite people in turn, the Christian grasping for cultural power and the Christian fleeing into a private holiness, and if your room only ever aims the indictment at one of them, you are leading half the study. So here is how you refuse the brawl in practice. Go first into every hard place. Before you ask anyone else to name where their final allegiance has slid toward a power they can see, name yours out loud, specifically, without softening it into a humble-sounding non-confession. When the render line tempts the quietists in the room to feel justified in their retreat, turn the knife toward them, because handing the public square to Caesar is not the same as rendering to Caesar. When the session on cultural power tempts the fighters to feel justified in their recapture, turn the knife toward them too, because a borrowed majority was never the kingdom. Even-handedness is not a tone you adopt. It is a discipline you practice in real time, catching the grasp in one session and the retreat in the next, and refusing to let the room aim the indictment safely at the people who are not present. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety and these are not safe topics. Safety here does not mean comfort. It means that a person can be wrong out loud without being humiliated, can change his mind without losing face, can say the half-formed honest thing without it being used against him next week. Set that expectation in the first session and guard it every session after. The facilitator script gives you words for this. Use them. The ground rules are not throat-clearing. They are the walls that make honesty possible. You will face three rooms, and you should know them before they arrive. The first is the angry person, the one who came certain this study is an attack on people like him, on his country or his church or the faith he was handed. Do not match his heat and do not rush to disarm him. Find the half of his anger that is true, because there usually is one, and say it back to him better than he said it, so he knows he was heard before he is answered. The grief over a closed store and a thinner world is real, and the people who sneer at it are committing their own sin. Grant that fully and mean it, and you will find the anger has somewhere to go besides escalation. The second is the hurt person, the one who is genuinely grieving the change in the country and hears the careful distinctions of this study as a dismissal of a loss that is breaking his heart. Do not argue with grief. Honor the person and the loss, and let the hard question stand beside the honor without canceling it. You are not there to win against his pain. You are there to show him that the truth and his grief can both stand in the same room, that he can mourn the real goods that eroded and still ask whether they were held by converted hearts or borrowed power. The third is the silent room, the one where nobody will go first because everyone is calculating the cost. The silent room is almost always a fear room, and the cure is not a better question. It is your own vulnerability. Go first, confess first, be unsure first, and the room will slowly follow you into the honesty you modeled. Silence after a hard question is usually people thinking, not people refusing. Count to ten in your head before you rescue it. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own heart. You cannot lead people somewhere you have not gone. If you walk into this study as the one who already sees clearly, the wise guide helping the confused congregation find its way out of idolatry or out of quietism, you have already failed, because the writer of these essays does not stand there and neither can you. Bell does not stand outside this. He has preached the render line as a permission slip and was wrong. He has flags on his own platform he has not moved. He grieves the Sunday-closed store he grew up with. He writes from inside the indictment, and the power of the whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, do the work yourself. Find the ordinary loyalty you have handed to Caesar without ever weighing it. Name the place your faith has been cheap because it was the default. Locate the incense you would burn to stay comfortable, or the lever you have trusted more than the cross. If you cannot find any of these in yourself, you are not ready to lead, because either you are without sin in this matter, which the gospel says you are not, or you cannot yet see your own, which means you will lead from above the room instead of inside it. The leader who has repented can call others to repentance without contempt. The leader who has not will turn the study into a weapon, however gently he holds it. One more practical word before the charge. Watch the clock and the temperature together. These sessions will run long if you let every objection become a debate, so you are not aiming to settle each question but to hold the room in the honest tension and then pray. When a conversation gets hot, slow your own voice rather than raising it, name what is true in what was just said, and move the table toward the practice and the reflection, because none of this lands as an idea argued. It lands as a thing carried out into the week. Trust the closing prayer to do work the discussion cannot. End every session there, even when nothing felt resolved, because Bell does not resolve these essays either, and a room sent out carrying weight will come back changed in a way a room sent out satisfied never will. Resist the urge to tie a bow. The unresolved ending is not a failure of the study. It is the design. Here is your charge. You are not the judge of this room. You are a fellow defendant who happens to be holding the readings. Lead like one. Let the weight of these sessions rest on you first and hardest. Refuse every chance to make this about the people who are not present. Keep the crucified King above every throne in your own heart before you ask anyone else to, and when you fail at it, say so out loud, because your failure honestly named will teach the room more than your competence ever could. The goal is not a room that agrees with you at the end. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who can give the coin back to Caesar and keep nothing of themselves in his hand, who can grieve what is dying without putting the church in the coffin, and who can no longer remember why they ever thought the kingdom came by holding the levers. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study just a way to tell Christians to keep their faith private and stay out of politics?
faq.a: No, and the study rules that reading out plainly. The render line was never a wall between faith and public life. It was a fence around a coin, and everything bearing God's image, which is nearly everything, sits on the side that belongs to God. The fourth session grants the whole case for engagement, that the prophets confronted kings, that a church which washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes. The error the study names is not engagement but the belief that engagement means seizing the throne. And it catches the opposite error just as firmly, the Christian who hands the public square to Caesar and calls the retreat holiness. If the study were only telling believers to go quiet, it would not keep turning to indict the quietist as hard as the crusader.

faq.q: Is this just a way to baptize political passivity and let the world run itself while Christians stay pure?
faq.a: It would be, if it spared the quietist, and it does not. The early church session refutes the retreat directly. The first Christians did not withdraw into a private piety. They built a visible society inside the old one, took in the discarded, stayed through plagues when others fled, and confronted the empire's idolatry to its face at the cost of their lives. Faith without power was not faith without engagement, and the church that attracts because it cannot compel is more public, not less. The study asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat by the name of holiness. A faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. Passivity gets no shelter here.

faq.q: What does render unto Caesar actually mean, if not keep faith out of politics?
faq.a: Jesus was handed a coin in a trap meant to get him killed, and he asked whose image was on it. Caesar's, so give it back to Caesar. But the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word Genesis uses for the human person made in the image of God. The coin bears Caesar's image and goes back to him. The person bears God's image and goes back to God. The line does not divide reality in half, with God minding the soul and Caesar minding everything else. It puts a fence around a coin and hands every image-bearer to God. So the question the trap springs on us is not whether you will pay your taxes. You will. It is what you have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his, your final allegiance, your sense of who holds history. Give the coin back. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.

faq.q: Is the end of Christendom really something Christians should not panic about?
faq.a: The study refuses both the panic and the celebration. Christendom is the social arrangement in which Christianity was the default of a civilization, baked into its laws and calendar. Christianity is the body of people who confess a crucified Lord. One is dying. The other has survived the death of empires before. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is partly the loss of advantage, the nominal and the convenient no longer pretending. But the study does not flatten the grief. It says grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those, because they are good. What it refuses is the assumption that the church is in the coffin. The seed is still in the ground, and the church grew fastest under a hostile empire with no cultural lever in its favor.

faq.q: Were the first three centuries of persecution really better than the church having power?
faq.a: The study is careful not to romanticize suffering, which it calls a kind of spiritual tourism when done from a comfortable pew. It traces the cost with dates and blood, Nero after the fire of 64, the martyrs of Lyon in 177, the empire-wide terror under Decius and Diocletian. The point is not to chase martyrdom or to wish the church back into the catacombs. The point is narrower and harder. The church did its clearest work and grew at its fastest rate when it had no power at all, because powerlessness made the love legible. When you cannot compel, you can only attract. That is not an argument that suffering is holy. It is a warning against assuming the church needs the safety and standing it did without for three hundred years.

faq.q: Does the two-kingdoms teaching tell the church to shut up while the state does as it pleases?
faq.a: That is the abuse the study names directly, the German error of the 1930s when two kingdoms became two sealed rooms and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. The doctrine done right reverses it. If the state is God's servant with a defined job, the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. The separation is not a wall protecting the state from the church's voice. It is the vantage from which the church can tell Caesar he is not God. The Confessing Church said it at Barmen in 1934, that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word we must obey. Two kingdoms, one Lord. A church that knows it is a different kingdom is the only one that can prophesy to this one.

faq.q: If the gospel is true, should the church not use political power to make the country righteous?
faq.a: The study rules this out at the cross. The church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it, told Peter to put it away, and conquered by being conquered. A gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. Jesus stood before Pilate and offered the absence of fighting as proof his kingdom is not of this world, because a kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. This is not a counsel of passivity. The two-kingdoms discipline means serving the city, paying the tax, honoring the office, working for justice, while keeping one foot in the kingdom of the crucified King, so that when the city asks to be worshiped, the church has somewhere to stand and the words to refuse. The error is not caring about the country. It is believing Christ needs Caesar's sword to finish his work.

faq.q: Is it wrong to grieve the loss of Christian culture, the closed stores and the moral consensus?
faq.a: No, and the study honors that grief as love looking at a wound. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn had more protection, the poor had more institutions tending them, marriage had more support. Those were real goods, and a flippant Christianity that celebrates their loss as freedom has stopped loving its neighbors. The harder question the study presses is how the church held those goods, by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery of compulsion. A protection that rests on a cultural majority rather than on converted hearts is always one election from collapse. The deeper work is forming a people who would live the mercy when the law no longer requires it, which is the only kind of strength the early church ever had. Grieve the wound honestly, then ask whether the goods were held by hearts or by power.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the leader and the writer instead of the real offenders?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the message. Bell does not stand outside any of this. He has preached the render line as a permission slip, he has flags on his own platform he has not moved, he grieves the Sunday-closed store he grew up with. He writes from inside the indictment, and the study asks every leader to do the same. The reason is not false modesty. It is that you cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue, and you cannot call others to repentance from a height without turning the call into contempt. A study that pointed only at the absent offenders, whether the power-grabbers or the retreaters, would let everyone present off the hook and change no one. By keeping the leader and the writer inside the indictment, the study makes repentance possible for the people actually in the room.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is this not just religion arguing about how to grab power either way?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by arguing against exactly the power-grabbing you distrust. The whole series holds that the faith of Jesus refuses to advance by seizing the state, that he turned down the kingdoms of the world when they were genuinely offered, that he took his throne by being executed and forgiving his executioners. If you have seen Christianity used as a tool for cultural power, the study agrees that is a corruption and names it as one, in the grab and in the smug retreat both. What it points to instead is the early church, which had no power for three centuries and grew anyway, by taking in the people the empire threw away. You do not have to accept the faith to notice the study is arguing against the very thing you are wary of.

faq.q: Does a kingdom not of this world mean Jesus did not care about justice here and now?
faq.a: No. When Jesus told Pilate his kingdom is not of this world, the proof he offered was the absence of fighting, his servants not taking up the sword. He was not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He was saying it does not come from this world's source and does not advance by this world's method. The same Jesus took in the discarded, healed the sick, and confronted the powers of his day with the truth, and the early church that followed him nursed the dying and refused to expose its infants. The kingdom reorders this world precisely by refusing to install itself through conquest. Caring about justice is not the error. Believing justice arrives only when our side seizes the throne is the error, because the cross shows the kingdom coming through what looked like defeat.

faq.q: Does refusing to fight the culture war mean I have to retreat into a Christian bubble?
faq.a: No, and the study calls the bubble the mirror image of the culture war, not its cure. The community Bell points to is not a bunker. It is a society so distinct that the watching world is drawn to it, the kind that takes in the discarded and forms people who live differently in public. The early church had no cultural power and was the most visible thing in the empire, not the most hidden. Losing the levers is not the same as leaving the world. The choice is not between fighting to recapture the culture and fleeing it entirely. Both responses keep the church focused on its own power or its own purity. The third way is salt, lived in the open, distinct enough that a neighbor has to ask what makes you that way. Withdrawal is the salt deciding to stop being salt.

faq.q: Does this study tell me how to vote?
faq.a: No, and a study that delivered a voting instruction would betray its own argument. The series indicts the grasp for cultural power and the retreat from public life both, and refuses to baptize either as the kingdom. Its concern is not which lever you pull but where your hope rests and whether your faith can still rebuke the side it loves. Two believers who have genuinely kept the crucified King above every throne can still vote differently in good conscience, weighing competing goods and arriving at different judgments, because political wisdom is not the same as ultimate loyalty. The study asks you to honor the office while judging the officeholder, to hold your convictions as a Christian rather than a soldier, and never to put in an election the hope that belongs to Christ. What you do with the ballot after that is between you and God.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have no seminary training and no preparation time?
faq.a: You lead it the way it was built to be led, by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than argument. The added material gives you teaching notes, scripture studies, and a leader primer precisely so you are not improvising. But the real qualification is not training. It is willingness to go first, to be honest about your own heart, to keep the room safe for people who disagree, and to refuse to turn the study into a brawl. A leader who has weighed his own allegiances and found some of them handed to Caesar can guide this faithfully with no degree at all. A leader with three degrees who stands above the room will do it harm. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

timeline.event: Jesus is crucified under Pontius Pilate, having told the governor that his kingdom is not of this world and offered the absence of fighting as the proof, taking a throne by being executed rather than by force.

Fire sweeps Rome and Nero blames the Christians, beginning the first imperial persecution and the deaths of believers, including, by tradition, Peter and Paul, for refusing to grant Caesar the final loyalty.

Pliny the Younger writes the emperor Trajan from his province asking how to handle the Christians he keeps executing, not for any crime he can name but for their obstinate refusal of the small civic gesture.
The martyrs of Lyon are tortured and killed in the arena, recorded by Eusebius in unbearable detail, grounding the cost of faith without power in dates and blood rather than sentiment.
The emperor Decius requires every citizen to obtain a certificate proving they have sacrificed to the gods, forcing Christians to choose between a public gesture of loyalty to the state and death.
The Great Persecution under Diocletian begins, the last and most severe assault on the church, with scriptures burned and churches razed, only a decade before the whole arrangement reversed.

The Edict of Milan, issued under Constantine and Licinius, grants toleration to Christians across the Roman Empire and ends official persecution, beginning the long alignment of church and imperial power.

The Edict of Thessalonica under Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire, completing the shift from a persecuted faith to an established one in three generations.
Augustine completes The City of God, written as Rome falls, arguing that no earthly nation is the city of God and that two cities built by two loves are mingled together in this age.
Martin Luther's teaching sharpens the two-kingdoms distinction between God's rule through the gospel and his rule through the civil sword, a frame that would later be both used and gravely abused.

The Peace of Westphalia ends Europe's wars of religion and entrenches the modern nation-state, tying religious identity to the sovereign's territory under the principle that the ruler's religion is the land's.

The Confessing Church issues the Barmen Declaration, written chiefly by Karl Barth, rejecting the false doctrine that any area of life belongs to a lord other than Jesus Christ, against a church gone quiet before the German state.

Robert Bellah publishes Civil Religion in America, naming the shared rituals and beliefs through which a nation understands itself before the transcendent, an instrument that can humble a nation or flatter it.
Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon publish Resident Aliens, reading the end of the Constantinian arrangement not as a death to mourn but as the freeing of the church to be faithful again.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, this study was written to indict every tribe, including mine and yours, so we are not here to score points against the people who want to grab the culture or the people who want to flee it. Both are in the room, at least in our hearts. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, the writer puts himself inside everything he says, the render line he preached wrong, the flags he has not moved, the Sunday store he misses, and so will we. We are not pointing from a safe distance. We are standing in it. Tonight we are looking at this theme together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the essay says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Bell does not resolve it either and neither should we. Take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

bibliography.title: The City of God Against the Pagans
bibliography.author: Augustine
bibliography.note: The two cities built by two loves, mingled in history until the end, so no earthly nation is the city of God. Written after Rome fell in 410. The deep background for sessions 4 and 5 and the spine of the two-kingdoms tradition.

bibliography.title: The Christians as the Romans Saw Them
bibliography.author: Robert Louis Wilken
bibliography.note: Shows how educated Romans like Celsus and Porphyry read the church as a stubborn, antisocial sect that withheld the small civic gesture holding society together. The fair statement of Rome's case in sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Rise of Christianity
bibliography.author: Rodney Stark
bibliography.note: Argues the church grew through plagues because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while others fled, so the math of who survived and who was loved did the rest. The empirical engine of session 3.

bibliography.title: The Ecclesiastical History
bibliography.author: Eusebius
bibliography.note: The early church's own record of the persecutions, including the martyrs of Lyon in 177 in unbearable detail. Grounds the cost of faith without power in session 3 with dates rather than sentiment.

bibliography.title: The Letters of the Younger Pliny
bibliography.author: Pliny the Younger
bibliography.note: The governor's letter to Trajan around 112 asking how to handle the Christians he kept executing for their obstinacy. The primary-source doorway into session 3.

bibliography.title: The Desire of the Nations: Rediscovering the Roots of Political Theology
bibliography.author: Oliver O'Donovan
bibliography.note: Makes the serious case that the gospel genuinely reshaped political authority, that the West was bent by Christianity into new shapes of mercy and law. Used to honor the strong defense of Christendom in sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: Practice in Christianity
bibliography.author: Soren Kierkegaard
bibliography.note: Names the great illusion of Christendom, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross because everyone was already a Christian by default. Central to session 2.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: Source of the claim that the church does not have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy, and of the call to read the end of the Constantinian arrangement as opportunity rather than only loss. Anchors sessions 2 and 5. Handle as one strong voice among several, since Bell also affirms public engagement.

bibliography.title: Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: Written after Newbigin came home to England in 1974 and found a pagan culture with Christian memories. Asks how the gospel addresses a culture that thinks it already knows what the gospel is. Frames the missionary question of session 2. Bell also cites Newbigin's The Gospel in a Pluralist Society on the absence of a neutral public square.

bibliography.title: The Myth of Religious Violence: Secular Ideology and the Roots of Modern Conflict
bibliography.author: William T. Cavanaugh
bibliography.note: Shows how the modern story of secular peace got told, with the state presenting itself as the cool referee that ended religious violence. Complicates the tidy two-drawer reading in session 1. Bell also draws on Cavanaugh's Theopolitical Imagination for the critique of the church as chaplain in session 5.

bibliography.title: To Change the World: The Irony, Tragedy, and Possibility of Christianity in the Late Modern World
bibliography.author: James Davison Hunter
bibliography.note: Documents how thoroughly the church lost its place at the cultural center and how poorly its strategies of political conquest served it. Grounds the diagnosis of session 5.

bibliography.title: Ethics
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's break with a two-kingdoms thinking that had decayed into two sealed rooms, written from inside the German church's failure. The conscience behind session 4. Leader to confirm specific chapter references before quoting, since the work is unfinished and compiled.

bibliography.title: The Barmen Declaration
bibliography.author: drafted chiefly by Karl Barth for the Confessing Church
bibliography.note: The 1934 confession that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word of God we must obey, and that there are no areas of life where we belong to another lord. The hinge of session 4. Leader to confirm wording and attribution, often printed in Cochrane's collection of Barth's writings.

furtherReading: Confessions and On Christian Doctrine, Augustine, for the fuller account of disordered love and the use of the earthly city that stands behind the two-kingdoms teaching in session 4.
After Christendom, Stanley Hauerwas, for readers who want to press session 2's claim that the church does not need to run the country, read with the study's affirmation of public engagement in mind.

Defending Constantine, Peter J. Leithart, for a serious counter-voice that resists the simple story that the church was ruined in 312, useful as a steel man against sessions 2 and 5. Leader to confirm.
Theopolitical Imagination, William T. Cavanaugh, for those who want to think harder about the church as its own public rather than a chaplain to the state.
The Rise of Christianity, Rodney Stark, for readers who want the social history behind session 3's claim that the church grew by staying when others fled.

glossary.definition: The line from Mark 12 in which Jesus tells the people to give the coin bearing Caesar's image back to Caesar and to give to God what bears God's image, the human person. Often misread as a wall between faith and public life. It is a fence around a coin.

The long social arrangement in which Christianity was the default setting of a civilization, baked into its laws, calendar, and manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church felt like the same act. Distinct from the faith itself, which can outlive it.

The pattern, named for the emperor Constantine, of the church aligning with state power after 312 and learning to advance its mission through the machinery of empire rather than through the cross. The founding bargain the study keeps returning to.

The teaching that God rules the world in two distinct ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross and through the civil order by law and the sword, so the two should not be collapsed into one. A discipline that holds a tension, not a wall that silences the church.

The shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself in relation to the transcendent, with its own sacred objects and holy days. It can humble a nation or flatter it, and it competes quietly with the worship owed to God.

The biblical condition of God's people living as a minority under a power not their own, told to seek the welfare of the city while never mistaking it for home. The posture the early church knew and the post-Christendom church is relearning.

Paul's language for the structures, authorities, and spiritual forces that order the world and can become idols when they demand the allegiance owed to God alone. The empire, the state, and the culture can each become one.

Augustine's image of the earthly city built by love of self and the city of God built by love of God, mingled together in this age so that no nation is wholly either one, distinguishable by their loves rather than their borders.

glossary.term: Salt that has lost its taste
glossary.definition: Jesus' warning in Matthew 5 that salt is useless once it dissolves into the dish and can no longer be distinguished from it. The image for a church so blended into its culture that it can bear witness to nothing beyond it.

Jesus' picture of the kingdom as the smallest of seeds that grows into a tree, promising life from smallness rather than ownership of the field. The corrective to a faith that mistook itself for the empire.

The movement within the German church in the 1930s that refused to fuse the gospel with the state, declaring at Barmen that Jesus Christ alone is the one Word of God to be obeyed. The case study of two kingdoms done right under pressure.

The witness of those who would not perform the small public gesture that signaled the state held their final loyalty, and died rather than give Caesar the last word that belonged to Christ. The blood that, Tertullian said, became the seed of the church.

Treating something other than God as ultimate. The idol is rarely a bad thing, it is usually a good thing, a country or a culture or a coin, asked to be God, which is exactly how an empire becomes one.
The biblical claim that the human person bears God's likeness, the eikon, so that every person belongs to God in a way no coin or empire ever can. The hidden answer Jesus gives in the render trap.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: From a coin held up to trap Jesus to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West, the church has always had to figure out how to live under power it does not hold. This five-session study walks slowly through what we owe Caesar and what we owe God, the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, and what is actually dying as the culture stops carrying us. It is even-handed, indicting both the grab for the levers and the retreat from public life, and it is built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Join us as we keep the crucified King above every throne.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study called Church and Empire, and before anyone braces for a political fight, hear this. It is not a campaign for a party, and it is not a call to abandon the public square. It catches the Christian who wants to seize the culture and the Christian who wants to flee it, and it implicates all of us. It asks a simple, hard question, what do we owe Caesar, and what belongs only to God. No homework, no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Give the coin back to Caesar. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand. A five-session study on how the church has lived under empire from Rome to right now, even-handed about both grabbing power and fleeing it, and built so anyone can lead it. Come honest, not finished.
quoteCards: The verse we use to make God small was spoken to make Caesar small.
Give the coin back to Caesar. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand.
Christendom is ending. Christianity is not. The seed is still in the ground.
When you cannot compel, you can only attract. Powerlessness made the love legible.
A church that grabs the sword forgets its Lord refused it.
Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second clause and you have lost the point.
We learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory won that way cannot be kept.
The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it.
